The investor Benjamin Graham borrowed the idea for his book The Intelligent Investor in 1949. He advised buying only when a price is well below what you think a thing is worth, so that you have room to be wrong. The same idea applies to ordinary life. Leave extra time for the trip, keep extra money in the account, and leave extra room in the schedule. A plan that works only when everything goes right isn't really a plan. The margin is what lets you survive the day that doesn't go well.

Everyone understands some things well and others hardly at all. Warren Buffett has said that what matters isn't how big your circle of competence is, but how well you know where it ends. A smaller circle with a clear edge is safer than a large one with a blurry edge.
Most expensive mistakes happen just outside the edge, where we know enough to feel confident and not enough to be careful. A good doctor may feel she can pick stocks, and a good engineer may feel sure about medicine. A useful habit is to say plainly, "That's outside what I know," and to find someone who knows it when the stakes are high. It's not an admission of weakness. It's a way of keeping your confidence tied to your actual knowledge.
The map is not the territory

In 1931 the scholar Alfred Korzybski pointed out that a map isn't the land it describes. A subway map is very useful precisely because it leaves out almost everything: the real distances, the streets above, the hills. It shows you how to get from one station to another and nothing more.
But try to find a particular building with it, and you'll see how little it tells you. Every model, chart, theory and statistic is a map. It helps you think, and it simplifies on purpose. It goes wrong when you forget that there's a real, messier world behind it. When a number on a screen disagrees with what you see out the window, it's worth remembering which one is the territory, and which is only a drawing of it.

Around 1896 the economist Vilfredo Pareto noticed that roughly 80% of the land in Italy was owned by about 20% of the people. The same lopsided pattern has since been noticed in many other places.
The 80/20 split isn't a law, and the real numbers vary from one case to the next. Sometimes it's 90/10, and sometimes it's closer to 60/40. The lasting lesson is that outcomes are often unevenly spread. A handful of customers, bugs or tasks can account for most of the results, so it helps to find which ones. If you can tell which twenty percent matters most, you can put your effort there, and stop feeling guilty about the rest.

The idea, popularized by Nassim Taleb, is that for things that don't age the way living creatures do, such as books, ideas and technologies, the longer they've survived, the longer they're likely to last. A book that has stayed in print for a hundred years is a better bet to still be read in another hundred than this week's bestseller.
Time acts as a filter. Whatever is still around has been tested by many generations, and has had many chances to be dropped. It's a rough rule, though, not a precise one. It doesn't apply to people, who really do wear out, or to things that physically decay. And a very old thing can still be replaced by something better. But as a first guess about which of two ideas will still matter in fifty years, the older one usually has the edge.

The physicist Enrico Fermi was known for getting reasonable answers to questions that seem impossible. A classic example is: how many piano tuners work in Chicago? You don't look it up. Instead, you guess the population of the city, the share of households that have a piano, how often a piano gets tuned, and how many tunings one person can do in a day.
Each guess may be off, but the errors tend to partly cancel, because some are too high and some are too low. The answer usually lands within a factor of two or three, which is often good enough to decide something. The real skill is breaking a big, scary question into small pieces that you can estimate. Many "I have no idea" questions turn out to be questions where you have a rough idea about each part.

For centuries Europeans took it for granted that all swans were white, because every swan they had ever seen was. Then in 1697 the Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh saw black swans in Western Australia. Thousands of years of observation had been overturned by a single sighting.
Nassim Taleb uses the phrase for rare, high-impact events that nobody expected and that we then explain as if they had been obvious all along. It's a warning about how much weight to put on a record of calm. A long run of ordinary days can tell you how things usually go, but not what's possible. One surprise can overturn thousands of ordinary days, and the sensible response is to prepare for what you can't predict, as well as what you can.

Some things are fragile and break under stress. Others are robust and simply hold up. Nassim Taleb's word "antifragile" describes things that get stronger when they are stressed, like muscles under a workout, bones under load, or immune systems exposed to germs. A teacup wants to be left alone, and a muscle wants to be challenged.
It's a helpful way of looking at systems, including our own habits. A life that avoids every difficulty may grow brittle, while one with small, manageable stresses can grow tougher. As a full scientific theory it's more a framework than something tested in detail, and it's easy to push too far, since not all stress helps. But the main idea, that some stress is useful, rings true in many places.

Many things are harmful in large amounts and beneficial in small ones, a pattern called hormesis. Exercise is an example. A moderate workout makes you stronger, while too much breaks you down. The dose makes the difference, and the effect isn't a straight line.
Some researchers suggest that fasting and sun exposure follow the same curve, with a bit helping and a lot hurting. In toxicology, scientists still debate whether low doses of things like poisons or radiation can actually help. So the idea is well supported in some areas, such as exercise, and still argued over in others. A cautious way to hold it is to remember that "more" isn't always "better," and also that "none" isn't always "safest."

In 1936 the sociologist Robert Merton published a short paper listing why actions so often have effects nobody planned. He pointed to ignorance of how things interact, mistakes in analysis, and what he called the "imperious immediacy of interest," meaning that people focus on the short term and what they want right now.
Policies, products and personal decisions all show it. A new safety rule may make people feel safer and take more risks, and a tax meant to discourage something may simply move it elsewhere. The takeaway isn't to avoid acting, since doing nothing has consequences too. It's to spend a little time on the second and third effects, and to try things small before you scale them up. That way the surprises, when they come, are cheap.

"Work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion." C. Northcote Parkinson wrote that line in a humorous 1955 essay in The Economist. He had noticed that the British Admiralty kept adding administrators even as the navy was getting smaller.
It rings true on a smaller scale. A task that you're given a week for tends to take a week, though it might have taken an afternoon. We find ways to use the time we're given, by polishing, rechecking or putting it off until the last day. A shorter deadline sometimes gets the same job done with less fuss. If you notice that your tasks are filling all the time you give them, try setting an earlier deadline, and see what happens.

Douglas Hofstadter wrote in his 1979 book Gödel, Escher, Bach: "It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter's Law." He was describing how long it would take computers to play chess at a high level, and the prediction was wrong in just the way the law says.
The joke is a recursion, because the law applies to itself. But it reflects a serious habit known as the planning fallacy. Our estimates are usually too hopeful, because we picture the job going smoothly and leave out the delays, the interruptions and the things that nobody thought of. A good rule is to pad your first guess, and then look at how long similar jobs have actually taken. Even then, it's wise to leave a little extra.

Fred Brooks managed the huge IBM System/360 software project, and in his 1975 book The Mythical Man-Month he wrote that adding people to a late software project makes it later. It sounds backward, since more hands ought to speed things up.
But new people have to be taught, which takes time from the people who already know the work. And every extra person adds more lines of communication, so more of the day goes to coordinating. As Brooks put it, nine women can't make a baby in one month. Some work simply can't be divided up. When a project is behind, it's worth asking whether the job really splits into parts that can go in parallel, or whether the wait is built in.

In 1969 Laurence Peter, an educator, wrote a funny book arguing that people in an organization get promoted for doing well until they reach a job they can't do well, and there they stay. He meant it as a joke, but he was pointing at something that many people have noticed.
In 2019 economists studied sales data on 53,000 workers at 214 firms and found a version of it. Companies tended to promote the best salespeople into management, where selling skills matter little. Good performance in one role doesn't guarantee it in the next, because the next job may call for different strengths. It's a reason for organizations to promote on the basis of what a job needs, and for each of us to ask whether we want the new role or just the title.

The first hour of study usually teaches you a lot. The tenth hour of the same day teaches far less. Each extra unit of effort, money or time tends to add a bit less than the one before it.
The French economist Anne-Robert-Jacques Turgot described it for farming in 1767: extra labor on a given plot yields smaller and smaller extra crops. Eventually another hour in the field adds almost nothing. It's a good reason to stop polishing at some point, and to spread your effort across more than one thing. The last five percent of perfection often costs more than the first ninety-five, and it's worth asking whether it's what you really need.

The philosopher John Rawls proposed a thought experiment in his 1971 book A Theory of Justice. Imagine you're designing the rules of a society, but you don't know who you'll be in it. You might be rich or poor, healthy or sick, talented or not, of any race or gender.
Rawls argued that you would then choose rules that are fair to everyone, since you could end up anywhere. It's a handy test for any rule or policy, big or small. Would you still endorse it if you didn't know which side of it you'd be on? A rule that only works for the person who wrote it is probably not a fair one. The veil is a way of borrowing other people's eyes for a minute.

A runaway trolley is heading toward five people on a track. You can pull a lever to divert it to a side track, where it will kill one person instead. Philippa Foot posed the puzzle in 1967. In 1976 Judith Jarvis Thomson added a version where you'd have to push a large man off a footbridge to stop the trolley.
Most people say they'd pull the lever but wouldn't push the man, even though the numbers are the same. Philosophers still argue about why. Some say it matters that pushing uses a person as a tool, and others say our feelings are leading us astray. The puzzle doesn't have an agreed answer, which is part of its value. It shows that our moral instincts aren't simply arithmetic, and that we can't always explain them.

The Greek writer Plutarch told of the ship in which the hero Theseus sailed home to Athens. The Athenians kept it for centuries, and as its planks rotted, they replaced them with new ones. Eventually every plank had been replaced.
Was it still the same ship? It's a puzzle about what makes something the same thing over time. Is it the material, the shape, or the history? Your own body is a version of it, since most of your cells are replaced over the years, and you still feel like you. The puzzle doesn't have a single answer, but it invites you to think about what you really mean by "the same," and about what it is that continues.

In his 1995 book The Demon-Haunted World, Carl Sagan gave readers a toolkit for spotting bad arguments. It includes seeking independent confirmation of the facts, considering more than one hypothesis, and asking whether a claim could in principle be proven false.
One of his tips is to avoid getting too attached to a hypothesis just because it's yours. He thought the tools should be used on yourself as well as on others, since the first person you're most likely to fool is you. The kit isn't meant to make you cynical. It's meant to give you a way to be open to surprising ideas without being gullible, so that you can say, with good reason, "That might be true, and here is how we could find out."

The phrase comes from a real job. When the Catholic Church was considering someone for sainthood, it appointed an official called the advocatus diaboli, who had to argue against the case and look for flaws. The role was ended by Pope John Paul II in 1983.
The idea is still useful. Before a big decision, ask someone to argue the opposite on purpose. If the plan survives a serious attack, you can trust it more, and if it doesn't, you've saved yourself a lot of trouble. The key is that the person is assigned the role, so they can disagree without being disagreeable. It's much easier for a team to hear "I'm playing devil's advocate" than "I think you're wrong."

A red team is a group whose job is to attack your plan, system or idea to see where it breaks. Militaries use them in war games, and companies use them to test their security by trying to break in. They are paid to be the enemy.
The reason it works is that the people who built something are blind to its flaws, because they know how it's supposed to work and so they use it the way it was meant to be used. An outsider doesn't, and will try things the builders never thought of. It helps to hire a friendly skeptic. You can use a small version of it at home. Ask someone to find the three biggest holes in your plan, and thank them when they do.

Experts make mistakes, not because they don't know enough but because complicated jobs have too many steps to hold in your head. In 2006 a team at Johns Hopkins introduced a simple five-step checklist for inserting central lines in Michigan intensive care units, covering things like washing hands and cleaning the skin.
Within three months, the median rate of line infections fell from 2.7 per 1,000 catheter-days to zero. The doctors already knew every item on the list. The checklist simply made sure that nobody skipped one on a busy day. It's a humbling result and a hopeful one. A short list can beat expertise alone, and pilots, surgeons and builders have all come to rely on them.

President Eisenhower, in a 1954 speech, quoted a college president who had said, "The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent." From that line, people later built a simple grid for sorting tasks into urgent or not, and important or not.
The most valuable box is the one for things that matter but have no deadline, like your health, your relationships and your long-term work. They're the easiest to put off, because nothing pushes you to do them. Meanwhile the urgent but unimportant things, like most emails and many calls, keep shouting. A week where you've done something from the important box, even a small thing, is usually a better week than one spent entirely on the urgent.

Before you know how something turned out, write down what you decided, what you expected, and why. It takes a few minutes. Later, when the result is in, you can go back and separate your reasoning from your luck.
You also can't tell yourself that you knew it all along, because the page says otherwise. It works directly against hindsight bias. Over months it shows you the kinds of decisions you tend to get right and the ones where you're too sure, which is hard to learn any other way. The entries don't have to be long. A line about what you chose, how confident you were and what you thought would happen is enough to be useful later.

The poker player Annie Duke uses the word "resulting" for judging a decision purely by how it turned out. A sensible bet can lose, and a reckless one can win. In a game with luck in it, the outcome of a single hand tells you little about how well it was played.
If you only look at results, you'll learn the wrong lessons. You'll repeat a lucky blunder and abandon a good plan after one bad break. A better question is "given what I knew then, was it a good decision?" That's harder to answer, because it asks you to forget what you know now. But it's the one that actually helps you improve, and it makes it easier to be kind to yourself when a good decision goes badly.

In 1956 the economist and psychologist Herbert Simon pointed out that people rarely find the best option. They find one that is good enough and stop. He called that satisficing, a blend of "satisfy" and "suffice."
Later, Barry Schwartz and his colleagues found that people who try to find the best, whom they called maximizers, often feel less satisfied with their choices and more regret, even when they've done well by objective measures. Not every study agrees with that finding, so it isn't settled. But "good enough" is often a wise place to stop. When the stakes are small, the time spent hunting for the perfect choice can cost more than the difference it makes.

When you're stuck on a decision, imagine how you'll feel about it in ten minutes, ten months and ten years. The writer Suzy Welch popularized the method in 2009. It pulls your attention out of the heat of the moment and gives you a longer view.
The urge to send an angry message may feel overwhelming in ten minutes, and in ten months it may seem trivial. The choice between two job offers might look different over ten years than it does today. It's a quick way to check your priorities, and it works because it makes you consider the same choice from three different distances. The answers don't always agree, and that disagreement is often the useful part.

In a letter to shareholders, Jeff Bezos described two kinds of decisions. Some are one-way doors, which are hard or impossible to undo. Others are two-way doors: if you walk through and don't like what's on the other side, you can go back.
Most decisions are the second kind, and they can be made quickly, with less than complete information. Save your slow, careful thinking for the one-way doors, like a marriage, a big loan or a surgery. And try not to treat every choice as though it were permanent. Many of us spend as long choosing a restaurant as choosing a house, and the restaurant can be changed next week. Sorting your choices by whether they can be undone makes it easier to spend your worry where it counts.

We usually think about bias, which is when judgments are off in the same direction. Noise is something different. It's scatter, when different people, or the same person on different days, make different calls on identical cases. Think of four rifle shots that are spread all over a target instead of clustered together.
In a study at an insurance company, underwriters were asked to price the same case. Their quotes differed by 55% on average, and the executives had expected a difference of around 10%. The cost of that scatter is large, and it's hard to see, since each person only sees their own judgment. It's a good reason to rely on shared guidelines and to get independent opinions, and not to assume that one person's call is the call.

In 1907 the statistician Francis Galton visited a fair where people guessed the weight of an ox. He collected the 787 entries and found that the middle guess, 1,207 pounds, was within a percent of the true weight of 1,198. The crowd was better than almost any individual in it.
It works under certain conditions. People have to guess independently, and they have to bring different information and different mistakes, so that the mistakes cancel each other out. If they copy each other, or a loud voice sways the room, the effect disappears. That's why it's smart to collect opinions separately before discussing them. A group that talks first often ends up with one person's guess repeated many times.

When we plan a project, we naturally focus on its details and how things will go this time. Daniel Kahneman and Dan Lovallo called that the inside view. It's the view from within your own story, where every step looks manageable.
The outside view asks a different question: how did similar projects turn out? Bent Flyvbjerg's research on large infrastructure projects found that most go over budget and take longer than planned. So before you trust your own timeline, look up how long comparable jobs have really taken. It can feel like an insult to your plan, as though yours were an ordinary case. But the odds are that it is, and the outside view is a reliable correction.

The political scientist Philip Tetlock ran forecasting tournaments in which thousands of ordinary people predicted world events. A small group did consistently better than the rest, and better than many professional experts. They were not geniuses.
What they did differently was a matter of habit. They broke big questions into smaller ones, thought in probabilities rather than yes or no, and updated their views as new evidence came in. They also kept score, so they could learn from their misses. The skill seems to come from ways of thinking, not from special talent, and that suggests it can be learned. Most of us make predictions all the time, and few of us ever check how well we do.

How do you grade a weather forecaster who says "70% chance of rain"? If it rains, were they right? If it doesn't, were they wrong? A single forecast can't settle it, since the forecaster said it might go either way.
The meteorologist Glenn Brier devised a score in 1950 that fixes this. Over many forecasts, a person who says 70% should be right about seven times in ten. The score rewards being well calibrated, and it punishes being very sure and wrong. It's a standard tool for judging forecasts of all kinds, from weather to elections. You can use the idea on yourself by writing down your confidence in a prediction, and checking later whether your 70% claims came true about 70% of the time.

The science fiction writer Theodore Sturgeon is said to have been told, in the 1950s, that ninety percent of science fiction is crud. His reply was that ninety percent of everything is crud. The remark has been repeated ever since as a rule of thumb.
It's a joke, and it's also a useful reminder. When you judge a whole field by its average, you'll be disappointed, because most of any field is mediocre. Judge it by its best, and you'll find what draws people to it. The same goes for books, movies, music and even your own ideas. Most of what you produce won't be great, and the way to get something good is to make a lot and keep the best.

C. Northcote Parkinson imagined a committee with a short agenda. It approves a huge nuclear reactor in a couple of minutes, since few members understand it well enough to object. Then it spends an hour arguing about the bicycle shed, because everyone has an opinion about that.
People devote most attention to the matters they feel competent about, which are often the least important. Big decisions are hard to understand, so we let them pass, and small ones are easy to understand, so we fight over them. In a meeting, it's worth asking whether the time spent matches the stakes. A rough check is to see what you've talked about the longest, and whether it was what mattered most.

When you're about to disagree with someone, first read their words in the most sensible way they allow. Philosophers use the principle so that they argue against the strongest version of a view and not a weak one. Neil Wilson named it in 1959, and Donald Davidson developed it further.
It also saves a lot of needless fights in ordinary life. Assume the person is reasonable until the evidence shows otherwise, and you'll often find they meant something different from what you first heard. Even when they didn't, you'll have a better argument, because you've answered what they said, and not a careless version of it. Charity isn't weakness. It makes you harder to dismiss, because you got the other side right.

Joseph Overton was a policy analyst at a think tank in Michigan. He observed that at any given time there is a range of ideas the public will accept as reasonable, and that politicians generally stay inside it. Ideas outside the window seem too extreme to be taken seriously.
The window shifts over time. Activists often work by pushing at its edges so that what was unthinkable becomes debated, and then what was debated becomes accepted. It's a helpful way of seeing why some policies are discussed and others aren't, and why opinions that once seemed fringe can become ordinary. It also helps to remember that the window describes what is acceptable to say. It doesn't tell you what is true, or what is right.

If the only tool you have is a hammer, it's tempting to treat everything as if it were a nail. Abraham Kaplan wrote in 1964 that "give a small boy a hammer, and he will find that everything he encounters needs pounding." Abraham Maslow later made a similar remark, and the saying is often attached to his name.
Experts do the same. The person trained in one method tends to see problems that this method can solve, and to miss the ones it can't. It's worth asking, when you're stuck, what other tools exist, and whether you picked this one because it fits or only because it's the one in your hand. Having a few different ways to look at a problem is often worth more than being very good at one.

A man is on his hands and knees under a streetlight, looking for his keys. A passerby asks where he lost them. "Over there in the park," he says, "but the light is better here." It's an old joke, and it describes a lot of real behavior.
We do something like it all the time. Researchers measure what's easy to measure, managers track what's easy to count, and we look for answers where it's convenient. What's easy to see gets more attention than what's important. If you notice that you're searching where it's easy, ask whether the thing you want is probably somewhere else. It may be dark over there, and you may need a flashlight, but that's where the keys are.

In a 1974 commencement speech at Caltech, Richard Feynman described islanders in the South Pacific who, after the war, built runways and wooden control towers and waited for cargo planes, as they had seen the military do. They copied the form of what they'd seen and none of the substance, so no planes came.
He said some research is like that. It looks like science, with the experiments, the charts and the language, but lacks a kind of utter honesty, including reporting anything that might show you're wrong. The point is that following the outward steps of a method isn't the same as practicing it. What matters is the willingness to find out you're mistaken, and to say so. That applies to anyone trying to learn what's true, not only to scientists.
You are the easiest person to fool

In the same 1974 Caltech speech, Richard Feynman said: "The first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool." It's the heart of how he thought science should work.
You have to be harder on your own ideas than you'd be on anyone else's, because you want them to be true. Wanting is what makes us careless. In practice that means looking for how you might be wrong first, checking the results that disagree with you, and being glad when you find out. It's an uncomfortable habit and a freeing one, because once you stop needing to be right, you're free to get closer to what's true.

Greek and Roman speakers who had to deliver long speeches with no notes used a trick that memory champions still rely on today. You pick a place you know well, like your own house, and in your mind you set each thing you want to remember at a spot along a walk through it. The stranger and more vivid the image, the better it holds. A loaf of bread on the doormat, a giant telephone in the hallway, a fish swimming in the sink.
To recall the list, you simply walk the route again and look at each spot. In a 2017 study, people who trained with the method for six weeks went from remembering about 26 of 72 words to about 62. Nothing about their brains had changed. They had learned to hang new information on a place they already knew by heart, and that is something almost anyone can do.

Working memory can only hold a few items at once, so the trick is to make each item bigger. A phone number grouped as 555-0142 is easier to hold than seven loose digits, because the grouping turns many pieces into a few.
A classic study with chess players shows how far this can go. Chess masters could recall the positions of pieces on a board from a real game far better than beginners could, but they were no better at all with pieces placed at random. They weren't remembering more pieces. They were seeing familiar patterns, and each pattern counted as a single item. That's what expertise often is, a large stock of chunks. When you're learning something new, look for the groupings, because they are what let the details fit in your head.

In 1971 the psychologist Allan Paivio proposed that we store words and pictures in two linked systems in the mind. If you learn something both ways, you end up with two routes back to it, and when one fails, the other may still work.
That's why it helps to sketch a diagram of what you've read, or to picture an idea, instead of only rereading the words. The picture doesn't need to be good, and it doesn't need to be neat. Making it forces you to decide what the thing actually means, how the parts connect and what goes where, and that thinking is half the benefit. A shaky drawing of how a heart pumps blood will often stay with you longer than a clean paragraph about it.

In 1975 Fergus Craik and Endel Tulving showed people a series of words and asked about each one of three kinds of question. Is it written in capital letters? Does it rhyme with something? Does it fit in this sentence? Afterward, the people who had thought about meaning remembered far more of the words than those who had only looked at the letters or the sound.
The lesson is that how deeply you think about something matters more than how long you look at it. Rereading is shallow, because your eyes move over words you already recognize. Explaining is deep, because you have to understand a thing to put it in your own words. If you want a fact to stick, try asking what it means, why it's true or how it connects to something else you know, and let the answer carry the memory.

A 1977 study asked people to judge words in different ways. For some words, the question was "Does this word describe you?" For others, it was about the word's meaning, or about whether it described someone else. Later, the people who had asked themselves the question about their own lives remembered more of the words than any other group.
Linking new information to yourself turns out to be a strong aid to memory, perhaps because you already have so much stored about yourself that there is plenty to attach to. When you study, ask yourself how an idea connects to something you've lived or done. If you're learning about habits, think of one of your own. If it's about the history of a city you've visited, picture the street. The more personal the hook, the harder it is to lose.

Endel Tulving and Donald Thomson found in 1973 that memory works best when the situation at recall resembles the situation at learning. In their experiments, a cue word that was present when someone learned a word helped them recall it better than a strong cue they hadn't seen before. A cue that was less obviously linked in the abstract could beat a cue that seemed better, as long as it had been there at the time.
It suggests that you should practice under conditions that look like the test. If the exam is in a quiet room, studying at a desk in silence may serve you better than studying lying on a couch with music playing. It also explains why something you can't recall can pop back when you return to the place where you learned it. The memory was stored along with its surroundings.

In 1975 Duncan Godden and Alan Baddeley had scuba divers learn lists of words either on a beach or underwater. Then they asked the divers to recall them either in the same place or in the other one. The divers did better when they were in the same setting where they had learned.
It sounds appealing, and it fits with what many of us feel when we walk into an old school and remember things. But later attempts to repeat the experiment have found that the effect is small and doesn't always show up. In 2021 one team reported that it didn't replicate at all in their hands. The effect seems more reliable when the place actually shapes what you were thinking about at the time. So don't count on a particular room to help you, but don't be surprised if it sometimes does.

Practicing some of what you know can make you worse at related things you didn't practice. In a 1994 experiment, Michael Anderson and his colleagues had people practice recalling some of the items in a category, like fruits. Later, they were worse at remembering the other fruits than they were at items from categories they hadn't practiced at all.
The idea is that when your mind picks one memory out of a group, it holds back the competitors, so that they don't intrude. That's helpful while you are searching, and it has a side effect afterward. The competitors become a bit harder to reach. It's a reason to review all of the material when you study, not just the parts you find easy or enjoyable, and to be a little wary of going over the same favorite examples again and again.

In 1974 Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed people films of car accidents. Afterward they asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed into" each other, or when they "hit" each other. The people who heard "smashed" gave higher speeds, an average of 40.8 miles per hour against 34.0 for those who heard "hit."
A week later, the "smashed" group was also more likely to say they had seen broken glass, though there hadn't been any. A single word in a question had changed what they remembered. It shows that memory isn't a recording that we play back. It's more like a reconstruction, and it can take in suggestions from the way we're asked. It's a good reason to be careful with leading questions, especially when someone is trying to remember something important.

In 1995 Elizabeth Loftus and Jacqueline Pickrell asked adults to read four short stories about their own childhoods, written with the help of their relatives. Three of the stories were true, and one was invented: that they had been lost in a shopping mall as a child and rescued by an older woman.
About a quarter of the participants came to remember the made-up event, and some added details of their own. Vivid, detailed memories feel reliable, and we trust them. But a detailed memory can still be wrong, and a confident memory isn't always a true one. This doesn't mean that memories can't be trusted at all. Most of our ordinary memories are accurate enough. It means that how sure and how vivid a memory feels is not a good test of whether it happened.

When something shocking happens, we feel as though we'll never forget exactly where we were. In 1986, the day after the Challenger space shuttle exploded, Ulric Neisser and Nicole Harsch asked students to write down how they had heard the news. Two and a half years later, they asked them again.
About a quarter of the later accounts were wrong in nearly every detail, and the students were still very confident in them. When shown their own original notes, some of them insisted that the new version was correct. The memory felt vivid, but the details had been rebuilt over time. Strong emotion seems to make us more confident in a memory, but it doesn't make the memory more accurate.

You can remember a fact and forget where you learned it. Daniel Schacter and his colleagues documented this in the 1980s, in patients with memory problems and also in healthy people. The fact survives, but the record of where it came from fades faster.
That's why a rumor you heard once, from someone you wouldn't have trusted, can seem like common knowledge months later. The content survives, but the tag that says "unreliable source" doesn't. If something seems like it's just something "everyone knows," it's worth asking where you first heard it. Sometimes you'll find that you can't say, and that's a good sign that you should check before repeating it.

Sometimes you can come up with an idea or a tune that you think is new, and it's something you heard before. In 1976 a US court decided that George Harrison had "subconsciously" copied the melody of the Chiffons' song "He's So Fine" when he wrote "My Sweet Lord."
The judge didn't believe that he had done it on purpose. A stored tune had simply come back to him without its label, and he took it for his own creation. Writers, musicians and scientists sometimes worry about it, and with good reason. It's a reason to keep track of where your ideas come from, to keep notes as you read, and to be a little modest about an idea that arrives suspiciously fully formed.

You know the word, you can almost taste it, and it won't come. In 1966 Roger Brown and David McNeill studied this state. People in it can often tell you the first letter and how many syllables the word has, which shows that memory stores words in pieces and not as a single lump.
Pushing harder often makes it worse, because you keep rehearsing the wrong candidates. The usual advice is to move on and let it come back by itself, which it often does a minute later while you're in the shower or washing dishes. It's a small reminder that remembering isn't always something we can order up. Sometimes the search keeps working in the background after we've stopped paying attention to it.

Remembering to do something in the future, like taking medicine or sending a message, is a different task from remembering the past. It usually fails because there was no cue at the moment you needed it. You meant to do it, you simply didn't think of it at the right time.
The solution is to attach the intention to something you'll definitely encounter. For instance, "when I pour my morning coffee, I'll take the pill." Psychologists call these implementation intentions, and they work much better than just resolving to remember. The idea is to decide in advance exactly when and where you'll act, so that the situation itself reminds you. A note on the door, an alarm, or a pill box on the kettle all do the same job.

A new memory is fragile at first and takes hours and days to settle. In 1900 Georg Müller and Alfons Pilzecker showed this with a simple experiment. People who learned a list of nonsense syllables and then immediately learned a second list remembered the first one worse than people who got a rest in between.
The first memory needed some quiet time to firm up, and the second list got in the way. Sleep is one of the periods when memories seem to firm up, which is a good reason not to cram all night. It's also a reason to leave small gaps in a study session, and to avoid starting something new and demanding right after you've learned something you care about. Your brain is still working on what you just gave it.

The old picture was that once a memory is stored, it stays fixed. In 2000 Karim Nader, Glenn Schafe and Joseph LeDoux gave rats a fear memory, then reminded them of it and blocked protein production in the brain. The memory was weakened, as if it had to be rebuilt each time it was recalled.
It suggested that recalling a memory opens a window during which it can be changed. That raised the hope that painful memories could one day be softened by treatment. Scientists are still working out how far this applies to people, and the results so far have been mixed. For now it's a promising idea and not a proven therapy. It does fit with the everyday observation that each time you remember something, you may be remembering your last remembering, and not the event itself.

In 1953 a surgeon removed parts of Henry Molaison's brain, including most of the hippocampus on both sides, to treat his severe epilepsy. The seizures eased, but he could no longer form new memories of facts or events. He met his doctors again and again as if for the first time.
Yet he could learn a new skill, like tracing a star while looking at it in a mirror, and he improved day by day without remembering that he had ever practiced. His case showed that memory isn't a single thing, and that the system for facts and events is separate from the one for skills. For decades he was one of the most studied people in science, and the knowledge gained from him shaped how we understand the brain.

You can know that something is the case, like the capital of France, and you can know how to do something, like ride a bicycle. Psychologists call the first declarative memory and the second procedural, and they seem to depend on different brain systems.
You might be able to ride perfectly well without being able to explain how you balance. Or you might know the steps of a skill and be unable to do it. People with amnesia often keep their skills while losing their memory of learning them. It's also why you can't learn to ride a bike by reading about it. The knowing-how part has to be built through practice, and reading only gives you the knowing-that.

In 1972 Endel Tulving suggested that we have two kinds of long-term memory for information. Episodic memory holds events from your own life, such as your last birthday party, and it comes with the feeling of being there. You can mentally travel back to it.
Semantic memory holds facts about the world, such as that Paris is the capital of France, without remembering when or where you learned them. The two usually work together. A memory of a trip draws on both what happened and what you know about the place. In some forms of amnesia one is damaged more than the other, and a person can know facts about their life while being unable to relive it. The distinction helps explain why a fact can feel like part of you, or not.

In 1974 Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch proposed that thinking in the moment uses several parts. There's a phonological loop for sounds and words, a visuospatial sketchpad for images and locations, and a central executive that directs attention among them.
The model explains why you can listen to music while reading a map, but find it hard to read an email while someone is talking to you. Tasks that use the same part compete, and tasks that use different parts mostly don't. It also suggests a practical rule. When you have a lot to hold in mind, don't pile more words on top of words. Draw a picture, make a list or use another channel to give your overworked loop a rest.

John Sweller suggested in the 1980s that, because working memory is so small, teaching should avoid wasting it. Making someone hold too much at once leads to confusion and poor learning, however good the material is.
One common problem is split attention. A diagram appears on one page and its explanation three pages later, so the learner has to keep flipping back and holding pieces in mind. Putting the explanation right beside the picture lets the learner spend their limited memory on understanding. It's a reminder that making something harder to read isn't the same as making it deeper. Clear presentation leaves more room for the thinking that actually builds knowledge.

If you're new to a subject, studying solved problems can teach you more than trying to solve them yourself. John Sweller and Graham Cooper showed this with algebra in 1985. Students who studied worked examples learned faster than those who spent the same time on practice problems.
Seeing every step frees your mind from searching for a method, and lets you notice the pattern in how the answer was built. As you get better, you should switch to solving problems on your own. The best sequence usually starts with an example and moves gradually toward independence, with the steps filled in less and less. It may feel like cheating to read the answer first, but for a beginner it's often the fastest way to understand.

Something that helps a beginner can get in the way of an expert. Step-by-step guidance with detailed explanations supports a novice, but for someone who already knows the material, it's redundant and can slow them down. They have to process the explanation and also check it against what they know.
Slava Kalyuga and his colleagues described the effect in 2003. It's a reminder that good teaching adapts to the learner. The same worksheet that rescues one student may bore another, and the same advice can help a beginner and annoy an expert. So when you're learning, it's worth checking where you stand. If the material feels like it's spelling out things you already know, try a harder version of it.

The Russian psychologist Lev Vygotsky, writing in the 1930s, described the distance between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with help. He thought the best teaching works in that gap.
If a task is too easy, nothing is learned. If it's too hard, the learner gives up. In between, with a little guidance that is gradually withdrawn, is where growth happens. It's a helpful way to think about your own learning, as well as about teaching someone else. If you're bored, move up a step. If you're lost, look for a small piece of help, like an example or a hint, and then try again by yourself.

A scaffold on a building holds things up until the structure can stand without it. In 1976 David Wood, Jerome Bruner and Gail Ross borrowed the word for the support a tutor gives a child. The tutor does the parts the child can't yet manage, such as holding the pieces in place, and hands over more and more as the child improves.
Good scaffolding is meant to be temporary. If it never comes down, the learner never learns to stand. This is useful to remember when helping someone with homework or a new job. Giving the answer teaches little, and walking away teaches little too. What works is to do just enough, then do a little less each time, until the person doesn't need you.

Benjamin Bloom suggested in 1968 that students should master each step before moving to the next, with extra help and time if they need it, instead of moving on with gaps. In a regular class, the lesson moves on whether or not everyone has understood, and the gaps pile up.
In 1984 Bloom reported a "two sigma" finding: students who were tutored one-on-one with mastery methods did about two standard deviations better than those in a regular class. That's a very large difference. Later studies have found smaller gains, so it's probably not as dramatic as it first appeared. But the effect is real, and it's why practicing the basics until they're solid pays off. A shaky foundation makes every later step harder than it needs to be.

In 1972 the German science writer Sebastian Leitner described a simple way to schedule flashcards using a few boxes. All new cards start in box one. When you get one right, it moves up to the next box, which you review less often. When you get one wrong, it goes back to box one.
The result is that the cards you know well get less of your time, and the ones you struggle with come back more often. It's a way of spending your effort where it's needed. You can do it with shoeboxes and index cards, and many flashcard apps use the same idea in software. The principle is the same as spaced repetition. Each success earns a longer wait, and each failure earns a short one.

In 2014 Pam Mueller and Daniel Oppenheimer found that students who took notes by hand did better on conceptual questions than those who typed. Their explanation was that typists copy more word for word, while writers, who can't keep up, have to summarize in their own words, and summarizing is a form of thinking.
Later attempts to repeat the study found smaller differences, or none at all, so the result is less firm than it was once reported. It may depend on how you take notes. Typing and thinking about the meaning probably beats handwriting and copying. The useful rule is not about the tool. It's that notes made by putting an idea in your own words will serve you better than a transcript.

Courses promise to teach you to read at 1,000 words a minute or more with full understanding. In 2016 a team of reading researchers led by Keith Rayner reviewed the evidence and concluded that it doesn't hold up. The claims fall apart when you test what readers actually understood.
There's a trade-off between speed and comprehension. You can skim, and skimming is useful for finding the main points or deciding what's worth reading. But it's a different task from reading, and you miss details. A normal speed for adults is about 200 to 300 words a minute. If you need to read faster, the better ways are to read more, build your vocabulary, and decide what you don't need to read at all.

In 2010 Colin MacLeod and his colleagues found that people remembered words better when they read them aloud than when they read them silently. The words they had spoken were more likely to be recalled later.
Hearing your own voice adds another feature to the memory, something distinctive about that item that sets it apart from the others. It works best for the things you most want to remember, because if you read everything aloud, nothing stands out. So reading key points aloud, even quietly to yourself, can help. It's an easy trick to try when you're studying alone, and it asks nothing of you but a little courage to talk to the room.

In the late 1980s Francesco Cirillo, then a university student, used a tomato-shaped kitchen timer to break his work into 25-minute blocks with short breaks between them. The technique is named for the Italian word for tomato, pomodoro.
It gives a clear start and a clear end to each session, and that can make it easier to begin, since twenty-five minutes feels doable. It may help some people focus. But there's little controlled research to show that twenty-five minutes is the right length, so it's best seen as a handy habit and not a scientific rule. Adjust it to what works for you, and if you're in a good stretch of work, there's no law that says you have to stop.

Does learning one skill help with another? In 1901 Edward Thorndike and Robert Woodworth tested it and found that practicing one kind of judgment, such as estimating the area of rectangles, did little to improve performance on others. The training stayed attached to the task it was trained on.
They suggested that transfer happens mostly when two tasks share the same elements. It's a sober point for anyone hoping that a hobby, such as chess or Latin, will make them smarter in general. Skills usually carry over only to similar tasks. That doesn't make such hobbies a waste, since they're worth doing for their own sake. It just means that if you want to get better at something, the best practice is the thing itself.

It seems sensible to keep practicing after you've got something right, to be sure. In a 2005 study by Doug Rohrer and his colleagues, students learned geography facts and then either stopped or kept drilling the same facts in the same session.
A week later, the extra drilling made no difference to how much they remembered. The time wasn't harmful, but it wasn't useful either. The better use of time is to come back to the material later, after some forgetting has set in, and practice it again. That's the thinking behind spaced practice. Instead of stacking more repetitions on the same day, spread them out, and each return will do more work.

To learn a foreign word, find an English word that sounds like it, then make a picture that connects the two. For the Spanish word "pato," meaning duck, you might imagine a duck wearing a pot on its head. The sound gets you from "pato" to "pot," and the picture gets you from "pot" to duck.
Richard Atkinson and his colleagues tested the method in the 1970s and found that students using it learned vocabulary faster at first. It works best for concrete words, which are easy to picture, and it's less helpful for abstract ones. Some research suggests the advantage fades over longer periods unless the words are practiced. It's a good way to get a word into your head quickly, and then regular use has to keep it there.

In 2003 Eleanor Maguire and her colleagues scanned the brains of people who rank among the best memorizers in the world. They found no unusual structure. These were ordinary brains, and they performed no better than other people's on general memory tests.
What distinguished them was how they remembered. Almost all used the method of loci, imagining a familiar journey and placing items along it. In other words, their results came from technique and practice and not from some special gift. That's encouraging, since it means a trained memory is available to anyone willing to put in the time. It also shows that "I have a bad memory" often means "I haven't learned how to use it."

Forgetting isn't always fading. Often one memory gets in the way of another. In 1924 John Jenkins and Karl Dallenbach had two students learn lists of nonsense syllables and then either go to sleep or stay awake. After the same number of hours, they remembered more after sleep.
When you're asleep, less new material comes in to interfere. Old things can disturb new ones, and new things can disturb old ones, and both happen all the time. It helps explain why you remember your own phone number but mix up the ones you used years ago, and why details from similar events blur together. Giving a memory some quiet time, or making it distinctive, can protect it from being overwritten.

Hermann Ebbinghaus, who started the scientific study of memory in the 1880s, noticed something. A list of syllables that he could no longer recall at all still took him fewer repetitions to learn a second time. He called the difference "savings."
The memory had faded, but it had not vanished. Something remained that made relearning quicker. It's an encouraging idea. If you've studied something before, even years ago, you'll relearn it faster than someone starting from scratch, even if you feel you've forgotten everything. So the time you spent isn't lost. A language from school or a math course you thought was long gone may come back more quickly than you expect.

In 1953 Colin Cherry studied how people follow one conversation in a noisy room, which became known as the cocktail-party effect. You can concentrate on one speaker and tune out the others, even when several people are talking at once.
Yet if someone across the room says your name, you often notice. So your attention filters, but not completely. Some of what you're ignoring is still being processed in the background, and something important or familiar can break through. It's one reason it's hard to concentrate in a busy place, and a good reason to find a quiet one when you're trying to learn something hard.

In the famous invisible gorilla study, people counting basketball passes often failed to see a person in a gorilla suit walk through the scene, pound its chest and walk off. They were looking straight at it. Their attention was simply somewhere else.
A similar thing has been found in medicine. In 2013 researchers asked radiologists to look for lung nodules in a set of scans. In the last scan, they had placed a picture of a gorilla about 48 times the size of a typical nodule. Most of the radiologists, 83 percent, didn't see it. Experts are not immune. We see what we're looking for, and we can miss a great deal of what's right in front of us.

We tend to think we'd notice a big change in our surroundings. In a 1998 field study by Daniel Simons and Daniel Levin, an experimenter stopped a pedestrian and asked for directions. While they talked, two men carrying a door walked between them, and as they passed, the experimenter was swapped with a different person.
About half of the pedestrians didn't notice that the person they were talking to had changed. They carried on giving directions to someone who was a different height, with different clothes and a different voice. We don't hold a complete picture of what's in front of us. We hold a rough sketch, and we fill in the rest, which is why a change can slip by unseen.

If you're watching a fast stream of images and looking for two particular targets, you'll often notice the first but miss the second when it comes within about half a second. In 1992 Jane Raymond, Kimron Shapiro and Karen Arnell described the effect and called it the attentional blink.
Processing the first target seems to use up your attention for a moment, so the next one slips past. It lasts only a fraction of a second, between about 200 and 500 milliseconds. But it's a fine illustration of how limited our attention is, even when we're alert and trying our best. Your mind isn't a camera that records everything. It's a spotlight, and while it's busy with one thing, the next may go unseen.

People often believe they can do two things at once. Mostly, they're switching rapidly between them, and every switch costs something. In lab experiments, people were slower and made more mistakes on the first trial after a change of task, even when they knew the switch was coming.
Part of the cost is that your mind has to drop one set of rules and load another, and part is that bits of the old task keep interfering. Doing one task at a time and finishing it generally takes less total time than bouncing between several. That includes checking messages in the middle of work. If you can, put your phone out of reach for a stretch and let yourself stay with one thing.

In 2010 Matthew Killingsworth and Daniel Gilbert built an app that pinged thousands of people at random moments and asked what they were doing and what they were thinking about. People's minds were wandering in 46.9% of the samples, and this was true whatever the activity.
They also reported being less happy when their minds wandered than when they were focused on what they were doing. Even when the daydream was pleasant, it didn't make people happier. That doesn't mean that all daydreaming is bad, since wandering can help with planning and creativity. But it suggests that a lot of our unhappiness has less to do with what's happening and more to do with where our attention is.

The psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi studied people who got completely absorbed in activities, such as rock climbers, chess players and surgeons. He called the state flow. They described losing track of themselves and of time, and of being wholly caught up in the task.
It tends to appear when a task is challenging enough to need all your attention but not so hard that it overwhelms you, and when the goals are clear and you get quick feedback on how you're doing. Time seems to disappear. It's one reason that matching difficulty to your skill makes work more enjoyable. If you're bored, raise the challenge a little. If you're anxious, make the task smaller until you find your footing.

In 1908 Robert Yerkes and John Dodson trained mice to avoid shocks and found that moderate shocks led to the best learning. Shocks that were too weak or too strong did worse. Psychologists later extended this idea into a rule that performance rises with arousal up to a point and then falls, giving an upside-down U.
Later work suggests that the best level depends on the task. Harder tasks do best with lower arousal, and easy ones can handle more. It's a rough guide and not a precise law, and the original study was about mice and shocks, not about people and deadlines. Still, it fits a familiar experience. A little pressure sharpens you, and a lot of pressure can make you freeze.
Sleep and the next day's learning

In 2007 Seung-Schik Yoo, Matthew Walker and their colleagues kept some volunteers awake all night and let others sleep, and then showed everyone pictures to remember. The next day, the people who'd been up all night remembered about 40 percent fewer of the pictures.
Brain scans showed less activity in the hippocampus, a region important for forming memories. So sleep matters for learning before you study as well as after. It's easy to think of sleep as time taken away from studying, but a tired brain takes in new things poorly. If you have a choice between an extra hour of cramming and an extra hour of sleep the night before you need to learn something, the sleep may be the better investment.

In 2003 Sara Mednick and her colleagues tested people on a visual task that gets better with practice. Those who had a nap of 60 to 90 minutes improved as much as people who had been allowed a full night's sleep. Those who didn't nap got worse over the course of the day.
A well-timed nap can restore some of your ability to learn. A short one of about 20 minutes may be better for just feeling alert, since it keeps you out of deep sleep and you wake up less groggy. If you're facing a heavy day of studying and you feel your mind getting dull, a nap can be a better answer than another coffee. It may not make up for a bad night completely, but it helps.

Videos for babies were sold in the 2000s as a way to boost their learning. In 2007 Frederick Zimmerman and his colleagues surveyed parents of infants aged 8 to 16 months. For each daily hour of baby videos, the children knew a few fewer words than babies who didn't watch them.
Researchers can't be sure the videos caused the difference, since parents who use videos more may differ in other ways. But the study gave no sign that the videos helped. What does help babies learn words is talking, reading and playing with the people around them. Babies learn language from conversation, with another person who is responding to them, and a screen can't do that. The most useful thing you can do is talk.

Endel Tulving and Zena Pearlstone showed in 1966 that a memory can seem lost until the right cue appears. People who couldn't recall a list of words suddenly could when they were given the names of the categories as hints. The memory was there, but they couldn't reach it.
That gives a different way of thinking about forgetting. Sometimes it isn't that the information is gone, but that you have no way in. It's a reason to leave yourself cues when you study, such as a keyword or a note in the margin. It also explains why a smell or a song can bring back a whole scene. It was part of the original memory, so it now works like a key.

In a well-known 2006 study, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke had students read a passage and then either read it again or take a test on it. The students who had reread felt more prepared. A week later, the ones who had been tested remembered far more.
Rereading creates a feeling of familiarity, and that is easy to mistake for knowledge. The words look known, so you assume that you know them. Testing yourself feels harder, and that's partly why it works. Bringing something out of memory strengthens it, in a way that reading it again doesn't. So when you study, close the book and try to say what you remember. The struggle is a sign that you're learning, not that you're failing.

You might think that guessing wrong would plant the wrong answer in your mind. In a 2009 study, Nate Kornell, Matthew Hays and Robert Bjork had people try to guess the answers to questions before being shown the correct one. Even when the guesses were wrong, they learned the right answer better than people who had just been shown it.
A wrong guess followed by quick feedback seems to prepare the mind to take in the answer, and the attempt makes you curious. So it's often better to try before you look, even when you don't expect to succeed. It also takes some of the sting out of being wrong. A mistake you notice right away isn't a failure of learning. It's part of how learning works.

Surprisingly, the more confident you are in a wrong answer, the more likely you are to remember the correction. In 2001 Brady Butterfield and Janet Metcalfe found that mistakes made with high confidence were corrected more often than those made with low confidence.
The surprise of learning that you were wrong when you were sure seems to grab your attention and fix the right answer in place. So there's no need to feel embarrassed about being wrong, especially when you were sure. A confident mistake is one of the best ways to learn, as long as you get the correction. What doesn't work is hiding the mistake, because then you never get the chance to replace it.

Aaron Beck was a psychiatrist who set out in the early 1960s to test a Freudian theory of depression and ended up noticing something else. His patients had a running stream of negative thoughts that they hardly noticed, and those thoughts seemed to be driving their mood. They would think things like "I always fail" or "nobody cares," and then feel exactly as bad as those thoughts would suggest.
He built a short, practical therapy around spotting those thoughts and testing them against the facts. It has since been studied in hundreds of trials, and it helps with depression and anxiety. Many of its tools can be learned from a good book, which is part of why it spread so widely. The core idea is gentle. You don't have to argue yourself into feeling happy. You only have to check whether the thought was true.

The thought record is one of the core exercises of cognitive therapy, and it is very simple. You write down a situation, the thought that came to mind, and how strongly you felt it. Then you list the evidence for the thought and the evidence against it, and you come up with a more balanced version.
The aim isn't to replace a bad thought with a positive one. A forced cheerful thought usually doesn't convince anybody, including you. The aim is to check whether the first thought was accurate, because it's usually only one of several ways to read what happened. A friend who doesn't call back might be angry, or busy, or ill. Writing the alternatives down slows your mind enough to see that the first story isn't the only one.

David Burns, who popularized Beck's ideas in his 1980 book Feeling Good, listed this one first among the common thinking traps. Things are either perfect or a failure, with nothing in between. "I missed one step in the plan, so the whole day is ruined."
Real life is mostly in the gray area, and so is most of what we do. A day can have a bad hour and a good evening. A diet can have a slip and still be a diet. A good habit is to catch words like "always," "never" and "completely," and ask what a more accurate description would be, such as "mostly went well, with one miss." It isn't a way of excusing yourself. It's a way of describing what happened without exaggerating in either direction.

A headache becomes a brain tumor. A late reply becomes the end of the friendship. Catastrophizing means leaping to the worst possible outcome and treating it as likely, and the mind can do it in a few seconds, with no new information at all.
One standard way to deflate it is to ask three questions. What's the worst that could happen? What's the most likely thing to happen? And how would I cope if the worst did happen? Answering them honestly usually shows that the worst case is unlikely, and that you would manage better than you fear. You don't have to talk yourself into believing that everything will be fine. It's enough to see that you have more options than the panic suggested.

"She didn't text back, so she must be angry with me." We often feel sure that we know what others are thinking, especially about us, and the guess is usually negative. It feels like perception, and it's actually a guess.
In truth, people are busy, distracted and mostly thinking about their own lives. Most of them are far less focused on you than you imagine. When you notice yourself mind reading, it can help to list other explanations for what you saw. If it matters, ask the person. A guess is not a fact, even when it feels like one, and a quick, kind question is often enough to replace a week of worrying.

"I feel guilty, so I must have done something wrong." "I feel anxious, so something bad is about to happen." Emotional reasoning treats a feeling as evidence about the world, as though the strength of the feeling proved the thing it seems to say.
Feelings do tell you something, but mostly about your body and your state of mind. Guilt can come from a rule you were taught long ago, and anxiety can come from too little sleep or too much coffee. A helpful move is to name the feeling and then check the facts separately, as if you were a fair-minded friend. You can take the feeling seriously without letting it be the judge. "I feel afraid" is true. "Therefore I am in danger" needs its own evidence.

Words like "should," "must" and "ought" set rigid rules for how we, or other people, have to behave. Aimed at ourselves, they produce guilt: "I should be over this by now." Aimed at others, they produce anger: "They should know better."
The psychologist Albert Ellis called this habit "musturbation," and he meant it to make people smile. The point was that rules which feel like laws of nature are usually preferences in disguise. Swapping "should" for "I would like to" or "it would help if" tends to keep the standard but drop the whip. You still care about doing well, and you can still hope others will behave well. You just stop punishing yourself and everyone else every time the world falls short.

One mistake becomes a whole identity: "I'm a failure," "I'm an idiot," "I'm unlovable." It's an extreme form of overgeneralizing, and it's harsh in a way we would never be with a friend. If a friend dropped a plate, we wouldn't tell them they're a disaster.
It also makes change seem impossible, because you can't change what you are. A label feels like a fact about your nature, so there's nothing to do but suffer. Instead, describe the behavior: "I made a mistake on that task." A mistake is something you did, and you can learn from what you did. That small switch in wording turns a verdict into a problem, and problems, unlike verdicts, can be worked on.

When something goes wrong, we may assume it's our fault, even when it wasn't mainly. A child has a bad day at school. A partner is in a mood. A team misses a target. The mind quickly asks what I did, and finds something.
Usually there are many causes: other people's choices, circumstances, luck. One way to see this is to write a pie chart of everything that contributed, and put your own share last. Most people find that their share is much smaller than the one they'd been blaming themselves for. This isn't about dodging responsibility. If your share is real, you can own it. It's about giving the right size to the part that is yours, and no more.

Albert Ellis taught in the 1950s that what upsets us isn't events themselves, but our beliefs about them. A is the activating event, B is the belief, and C is the consequence, the emotion. We tend to see A and C and miss B, which sits in between and does the work.
Two people miss the same train. One thinks, "This is a disaster, I'll be late and in trouble," and feels panic. The other thinks, "Well, time for a coffee," and feels fine. The event was identical, and the beliefs made the difference. That's good news, because beliefs can be questioned in a way that events can't. When you're upset, try asking what you were telling yourself in the moment before the feeling arrived.

When you're low, it's natural to wait until you feel better to do things. But the lack of activity makes the low mood worse, and a cycle starts: you do less, you feel worse, and so you do even less. Behavioral activation reverses it.
You schedule small activities that matter to you, such as a walk or a phone call, and do them whether or not you feel like it. Mood often follows action, and not the other way around. In a 1996 trial, activation alone worked about as well as full cognitive therapy for depression, and a later trial found it comparable to medication. It's a humble idea with solid support. You don't have to feel ready to begin. You only have to start with something small.

Marsha Linehan's dialectical behavior therapy includes a skill for when an emotion pushes you to do something that isn't helpful. Sadness says to hide in bed. Anger says to lash out. Fear says to avoid. Each emotion comes with an urge, and following the urge usually makes the feeling last.
Opposite action means doing the reverse in small ways: reaching out to a friend, being gentle, approaching what you fear. You do it with your whole attention, not grudgingly. It works when the feeling is out of proportion to the situation. It isn't meant to override feelings that fit the facts. If you're afraid of a real danger, avoiding it is wise. But if you're afraid of a phone call, making it will show your mind that the call is survivable.

Marsha Linehan draws a line between pain and suffering. Pain is what happens: the loss, the diagnosis, the end of the marriage. Suffering is what we add by fighting the fact that it happened, with thoughts like "this shouldn't be happening" or "it isn't fair."
Radical acceptance means fully acknowledging what is, in your mind and in your body. It doesn't mean approving, liking it, or giving up on changing things. You can accept that something happened and still work to make the future different. It means no longer spending your energy on the argument with reality, an argument that nobody wins. Pain is hard enough. Acceptance is a way of not paying twice.

In dialectical behavior therapy, there are said to be three states of mind. Emotional mind is driven by feelings and tends to be impulsive. Reasonable mind is driven by facts and logic, and it can miss what matters. Wise mind is where they overlap, the place where you know something is right and can feel it too.
Most of us have had moments like that, when a decision felt calm and true. Linehan teaches people to pause, breathe and ask from that place, "What do I really want to do here?" It's not a mystical idea. It's a way of putting your feelings and your reasoning in the same room and letting them both speak, before you act on either one alone.

When distress spikes so hard that thinking clearly is out of reach, Linehan's group suggests changing the body first. TIPP stands for Temperature, Intense exercise, Paced breathing and Paired muscle relaxation. Each one acts on your physical alarm state directly.
Cold water on your face, a minute of hard exercise or a long slow exhale quickly shifts your body out of its emergency mode. They're meant for the moments when you're flooded, not for solving the underlying problem, which you can tackle once you're calmer. Trying to reason with yourself at the peak of panic rarely works. First lower the volume with your body, and then take up the question again.

In acceptance and commitment therapy, you learn to treat thoughts as passing events in the mind, and not as truths. Instead of "I'm worthless," you say, "I'm having the thought that I'm worthless." It's a small change in wording, and it changes your relationship to the thought.
The thought may not vanish, but it loosens its grip, because you're now watching it instead of being it. It can sound like a small trick, but with practice it creates a little space between you and what your mind says, and in that space you can choose how to act. You don't have to win an argument with your own mind. You only have to notice that a thought is a thought, and keep doing what matters.

In acceptance and commitment therapy, a goal is something you can finish, like attending your child's recital. A value is a direction you keep moving in and never complete, like being a loving parent. You can tick off a goal, but you can't be finished with a value.
Goals can be missed, and then it can feel like failure. Values can always be lived, in some small way, today. When life has been knocked off course, as it can be by a divorce or a loss, asking what you value and what one small step fits it can show you where to go. Even on a bad day, there's usually some way to move in the direction you care about, even if it's only a kind word.

In 1979 Jon Kabat-Zinn started a stress clinic at the University of Massachusetts Medical School. Patients came for an eight-week course that combined meditation, body awareness and gentle yoga. Many of them had chronic pain or illnesses that medicine had not been able to fix.
It has been tested in many trials since. A large review in 2014 found moderate evidence that it helps with anxiety, depression and pain, about as much as other active treatments. It's not a cure-all, and it doesn't work for everyone, but it gives many people a skill they can keep using. The practice is simple to describe: pay attention on purpose, to the present moment, without judging it. It is much harder to do than to say.

Depression often comes back. Zindel Segal, Mark Williams and John Teasdale developed a version of mindfulness training meant to help prevent that, by teaching people to notice the early signs of a downward slide and not get pulled in.
In a 2000 trial, people who had had three or more episodes of depression were followed for a year. The relapse rate was 37% for those who took the course and 66% for those who got usual care. For people with fewer episodes, there was no difference. So the benefit was clearest for those with the most to lose, which makes sense, since those are the people whose minds have learned the path best. It's an encouraging result for anyone with a history of low periods.

In the 1980s James Pennebaker asked people to write about the most upsetting experience of their lives for 15 to 20 minutes on each of several days. Some later showed improvements in health, such as fewer doctor visits. The idea was that putting a painful experience into words helps the mind make sense of it.
Later reviews found that the average effect is small and varies from person to person. It's not a treatment, and it can hurt a little at the time, since writing about something painful brings it back. Still, it seems safe for most people, and many find that it helps them sort out what they feel. If you try it, write for yourself and don't worry about how it reads. Nobody needs to see it.

If you can't stop worrying, one method is to give worry its own appointment. Thomas Borkovec's work in the 1980s led to a technique where you pick a time, say 15 to 30 minutes in the early evening, and postpone your worries until then.
When one comes up during the day, you jot it down and tell yourself "later." Many people find that the urge fades by the time the appointed hour comes, and some of the worries no longer seem worth the time. During the appointment you can think about them as hard as you like.
