It works because the mind finds it easier to put something off than to be told to stop. It also teaches that worries don't have to be answered the moment they appear.

William Miller and Stephen Rollnick developed this style of conversation in the 1980s while working with people who had addictions. They noticed that arguing for change usually makes people argue back. The more you push, the more they defend what they're doing.
So instead, the helper asks open questions, listens carefully and invites the person to talk about both sides of their mixed feelings. When people hear themselves say why they might change, they're more likely to do it. It works well when someone is unsure, and it's useful in everyday life as well. If a friend is stuck on something, you'll often do more good by asking what they think than by telling them what to do.

In the 1980s James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente studied how people quit smoking and described a series of stages. In precontemplation, they aren't thinking about it. In contemplation, they're weighing it up. Then come preparation, action and maintenance.
Relapse is common, and it counts as part of the cycle, not as failure. Many people go around several times before a change lasts. Researchers debate whether the stages are truly distinct, and some studies have not supported the model in its strict form. But the idea that readiness matters is widely used. It reminds us that someone who isn't ready can't be pushed into it, and that we ourselves may be at a different stage for different things.

Edward Deci and Richard Ryan studied what keeps people motivated and found three basic needs. Autonomy is the sense that you're making your own choices. Competence is feeling capable at what you do. Relatedness is feeling connected to other people.
When these needs are met, people are more motivated, more creative and happier. The pattern holds across many cultures. It helps explain why pressure works poorly for long. It takes away autonomy, so even good activities start to feel like chores. If you want to keep up a habit, ask whether you've chosen it yourself, whether you're getting any better at it, and whether anyone shares it with you.

In 1966 Julian Rotter described a difference between people who believe their lives are shaped mainly by their own actions, and those who believe it's mainly luck, fate or other people. He called these an internal and an external locus of control.
An internal locus tends to go with better coping, healthier habits and more achievement. But the world isn't fully controllable, and an accurate sense of what is in your power matters too. Someone who believes they control everything can feel crushed when things go wrong. The useful skill is telling apart what you can influence from what you can't, and putting your effort into the first while making peace with the second.

Albert Bandura introduced the term in 1977 for your belief in your ability to do a specific task. It's different from general confidence. You might feel sure you can cook a dinner and unsure you can give a speech.
It predicts whether you'll try, how hard you'll work and whether you'll keep going after a setback. It grows mainly from small successes, from watching someone like you succeed, from encouragement and from managing your stress. That's practical advice in disguise. If you want to build your belief that you can do something big, set a goal you can actually reach, reach it, and then set the next one. Each success is evidence you can show yourself.

In the 1960s Martin Seligman and Steven Maier gave dogs shocks that they could not escape. Later, when the dogs could easily avoid shocks by jumping over a barrier, many just lay down and took them. It looked as though they had learned that nothing they did mattered.
In 2016 Maier and Seligman revised the theory. They concluded that passivity is the brain's default response to prolonged pain, and that what has to be learned is that you do have control. That's a hopeful reading. It suggests that helplessness isn't something we acquire so much as something we need to unlearn, and that even small experiences of making a difference can start to turn it around.

Martin Seligman found that people differ in how they explain bad events to themselves. Pessimists tend to see causes as permanent, personal and pervasive: "It will always be like this, it's my fault, and it ruins everything."
Optimists see them as temporary, specific and partly outside their control: "This is a rough patch, it's about this one situation, and some of it wasn't up to me." Explanatory style predicted sales success at an insurance company, and it predicted how people recovered from low mood. It can be changed with practice. The trick is to notice the words "always," "my fault" and "everything" in your own thinking, and to try a more precise version.

George Bonanno studied how people cope with losses like the death of a spouse. Many experts had expected most of them to go through a long period of deep distress, and to be worse off if they did not.
He found that the most common pattern was a short time of grief followed by a return to normal functioning, and that a minority did have prolonged difficulty. Being resilient doesn't mean not hurting. It means that people are, on the whole, sturdier than they expect. If you are in the middle of something terrible, it's worth knowing that most people who go through it come out the other side, and the odds are with you.
The dual process model of grief

In 1999 Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut proposed that grieving well isn't a straight line through stages. People swing back and forth between two kinds of coping. In loss-oriented moments, they face the pain, think about the person and miss them.
In restoration-oriented moments, they deal with daily life and new roles, and take breaks from grief. The back and forth is normal and healthy. Taking a break from sadness isn't avoiding it, and it isn't a betrayal of what you've lost. It's part of how people carry a loss over a long time. If you find yourself laughing at a movie in the middle of a hard month, there's nothing wrong with you.

Grief is not an illness. Most people find that the sharpest pain eases over time, even if the missing never entirely goes away. It comes in waves, and the waves get further apart.
For some, intense longing and distress continue for a year or more and make daily life difficult. In 2022 the diagnostic manual added prolonged grief disorder for that situation. It is a name for grief that's stuck, not a judgment about how much someone loved. It responds to treatment, which can help people find a way to live with the loss. If the weight isn't lifting after a long time, asking for help is reasonable, and it isn't a sign of weakness.

In 1996 Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun described how some people report positive changes after a crisis: closer relationships, a greater appreciation of life, new priorities or a stronger sense of purpose. They called it post-traumatic growth.
It's a real experience for many people. But not everyone has it, and no one should feel that they have to. Researchers also point out that people's own reports of growth don't always match how they're actually doing later, so the picture is uncertain. A fair way to hold it is that growth can come alongside pain, and doesn't cancel it. You can wish it hadn't happened and still be glad of what you learned.

Paul Amato, who has studied divorce for decades, describes it as a long series of changes, not a single event. Conflict before the split, the move, the finances, parenting arrangements and new relationships each affect how people cope.
Most adults adjust over time. But the path varies a lot, and the stress people feel depends heavily on what follows the separation. So how things go afterward is partly within your influence. A steady routine, a stable place to live and decent relations with your former partner can make a real difference to how you feel a year on. The first months are rarely a good guide to how it will go.
Most children of divorce do fine

E. Mavis Hetherington followed families through divorce for decades in the Virginia Longitudinal Study. About 75 to 80 percent of the children from divorced families were functioning well as adults, compared with about 90 percent of those from intact families.
So most children cope, though a minority struggle more, and the difference between 80 and 90 percent is real. What helped them was steady parenting, low conflict between the parents and a warm relationship with at least one adult. Those are things that a parent can work on, even in the middle of a hard time. The study doesn't say divorce is painless for children, but it does say that most children come through it, and that what happens afterward matters a great deal.

In 1985 Sheldon Cohen and Thomas Wills reviewed the research on how social support affects health. They found that having people to lean on protects against the harm of high stress. It is like a cushion that matters most when the blow is hardest.
What matters most is the sense that if you needed help, someone would be there. That perception may be as protective as actually receiving help. It's one reason that staying in touch with the people who care about you pays off during hard times. You don't have to be using them constantly. Knowing that they are there is already doing some of the work, so keep the calls and the coffees going.

In 2010 Julianne Holt-Lunstad and her colleagues combined 148 studies covering more than 300,000 people. They found that people with strong social relationships had a 50 percent greater likelihood of survival over the follow-up periods than those with weak ones.
The size of the effect was comparable with quitting smoking, and larger than that of obesity or inactivity. It's not just that the lonely are sicker to begin with. Connection seems to matter for staying well, though the research can't prove cause and effect. Still, it's a good reason to treat friendships as a part of your health and not as a luxury. A regular call or meal is worth planning, especially when life is hard.

Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough asked people to write weekly about things they were grateful for. In 2003 they reported that, compared with people who wrote about hassles, the gratitude group felt better about their lives and were more optimistic.
A later review found the average benefit is modest. So it's a helpful habit that costs nothing, though it isn't a cure for depression and shouldn't be used to push down real pain. It seems to work best if you write about specific things and about people, and not generalities. "My neighbor shoveled my walk" does more than "I'm grateful for kindness." Ten minutes once a week may be all it takes.

Martin Seligman and his colleagues asked people to write down three things that went well each day, and why they went well, for one week. In a 2005 study, those who did so were happier and less depressed for up to six months afterward.
Later studies have found smaller or shorter-lived effects, so the results are mixed. It takes only a few minutes a night, and many people find that it shifts their attention toward what's good, which can be hard to see on a rough day. The "why" part matters. Asking why a good thing happened reminds you of what you did, or what others did for you. It's a small thing, and worth trying for a week to see if it helps you.

Fred Bryant and Joseph Veroff, who wrote the book on savoring, describe it as deliberately paying attention to a pleasant experience so that you enjoy it more and it lasts longer. It's the opposite of rushing through a good moment on the way to the next one.
They suggest sharing it with someone, taking mental snapshots, and thinking about it afterward. You can savor the past through memories, the present through full attention, and the future through anticipation. It's a skill that can be practiced. Next time you have a good cup of coffee or a nice view, try giving it your full attention for a minute. Most of us have more pleasant moments than we notice, because we're busy thinking about something else.

The psychologist Dacher Keltner studies awe, the feeling you get before something vast that changes how you see the world. It could be a mountain range, a piece of music or a big idea. It is a mixture of wonder and a sense of being small.
In his research, awe makes people feel smaller in a good way, more connected to others and more generous. It also seems to quiet self-focused worry. You don't need a trip to the Grand Canyon to feel it. Walks in nature and looking at the night sky can do it, and so can a great piece of music or a story of someone's courage. When your own problems feel huge, a dose of something larger can put them in a different light.

Lisa Feldman Barrett found that some people describe their feelings with precision, telling "anxious" from "disappointed" from "ashamed," and others lump everything together as "bad" or "awful." She called the first skill emotional granularity.
The people with finer distinctions cope with stress more flexibly. They seem to have more options, since a precise label points to a particular response. Disappointment calls for adjusting your plans, while shame calls for self-compassion, and a vague "bad" calls for nothing in particular. Building your emotional vocabulary can be as simple as pausing to ask what exactly you're feeling. Often a better word is the first step to knowing what to do.

Walter Cannon, a physiologist at Harvard, described in 1915 how the body prepares for fight or flight. Your heart races, your breathing quickens and your muscles tense. Blood moves to your limbs, and digestion slows down.
The system evolved for physical danger, but it responds to an urgent email just as well. Freezing is another common response, when neither fight nor flight seems possible. The good news is that the system can be switched off. Slow breathing, a walk and talking with a friend all tell the body that it's safe to stand down. When you feel that surge in a situation that doesn't need your muscles, it helps to remember that it's an old alarm, and that you can settle it.

Bruce McEwen introduced the term in the 1990s for the wear and tear that builds up when the body's stress systems are working too much, or never switch off. A stress response is meant to be brief, a surge that rises and then settles. When it stays on, the surge becomes a drain.
Over time that can show up as higher blood pressure, weakened immunity and trouble sleeping. It isn't just about how big a stressor is. How long it lasts and how well you recover also matter. That means rest and recovery are part of managing stress, not a reward for finishing it. If you're going through a long hard stretch, treating sleep, meals and quiet time as part of the job is not self-indulgence. It's maintenance.

Christina Maslach, a psychologist, developed the best-known measure of burnout in the early 1980s. It has three parts. The first is exhaustion. The second is cynicism, or a feeling of detachment from the work. The third is a feeling of being ineffective, that nothing you do makes a difference.
It usually grows out of chronic stress at work, including overload, little control and a lack of recognition. The World Health Organization calls it an occupational phenomenon and not a medical condition. That wording points to something useful. Burnout is often addressed by changing the conditions, such as workload and support, and not only by asking the person to be more resilient. A tired person who is told to try harder is usually being given the wrong advice.

In 1978 Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes described high-achieving women who felt like frauds. They believed they had fooled everyone, and they expected to be found out at any moment. Later work showed that it happens to men too, and that it's very common.
It isn't a diagnosis, but it is a familiar feeling. People who feel it often attribute their success to luck and discount their abilities, while treating their failures as proof of the truth. One of the best remedies is talking about it with others. You'll often discover that people you admire feel exactly the same, which is a relief. It also helps to keep a record of what you've actually done, since the feeling tends to ignore it.

The technique is two breaths in through the nose, the second a small top-up, followed by a long slow breath out through the mouth. You repeat it for a few minutes. It sounds almost too simple to matter.
In a 2023 Stanford trial with 108 people, those who did five minutes of it a day for a month improved their mood and lowered their resting breathing rate more than people who did mindfulness meditation. The long exhale seems to be what calms the body. It's easy to try. A few rounds when you notice tension can take the edge off, and it costs nothing, needs no equipment and can be done at a desk or in a waiting room.

In 1977 Mary Lee Smith and Gene Glass combined the results of 375 studies of psychotherapy in one of the first meta-analyses. They found that the average person who had therapy ended up better off than about 75 percent of people who hadn't. At that time, some critics were still claiming that talk therapy did nothing.
Later reviews have reached similar conclusions. It doesn't mean that every therapy works for every person, and some people don't improve. It does mean that, on average, talking with a trained person helps, and it helps by a meaningful amount. If you've been wondering whether it's worth the time and cost, the evidence says that it usually is. The harder part, in practice, is finding someone who suits you.

Researchers have found that the quality of the bond between client and therapist, including agreement on the goals and the tasks of therapy, predicts how well the treatment works. A 2018 review of nearly 300 studies found a consistent link, whatever type of therapy was being used.
So if you're thinking about seeing someone, it matters that you feel understood and comfortable. A therapist can be well trained and still not be right for you. It's fine to try a different one if the first isn't a good fit, and doing so is not a failure on your part. It's the same way you'd choose a doctor or a teacher. The method matters, and so does the person delivering it.

In Alice in Wonderland, after a race, the Dodo declares, "Everybody has won, and all must have prizes." In 1936 Saul Rosenzweig borrowed the line to describe a puzzling finding that different forms of psychotherapy seem to work about equally well.
Later researchers, including Lester Luborsky, found similar results. Not everyone agrees with the verdict. For some conditions, such as phobias and panic, particular treatments do seem to do better. But the overall similarity suggests that shared ingredients, such as the relationship, a believable explanation and a plan, matter a lot. The debate hasn't been settled. A fair summary is that the method matters less than we might expect, and that the fit between the person and the approach matters more.

In 1936 Anna Freud, Sigmund's daughter, described the mind's habits for protecting us from painful feelings, such as denial, projection, displacement and rationalization. These are things we do without deciding to, and often without knowing.
The psychiatrist George Vaillant later ranked them from immature, like denial, to mature, like humor and sublimation. The ideas are useful for describing how people cope, and many therapists use them. But the research behind them is mostly observation and not controlled experiment, so they're better thought of as helpful descriptions than as proven mechanisms. It's still worth asking, when you've reacted strongly, whether you were protecting yourself from something you didn't want to look at.

When we can't safely express a feeling at its source, we sometimes aim it at someone safer. A man is humiliated by his boss, says nothing, and then snaps at his family when he gets home. The anger was real, but it landed on the wrong people.
It's one of the classic defense mechanisms, and almost everyone has seen it at work. Spotting it can help. When your reaction seems bigger than the situation, ask yourself who or what the feeling is really about. Often the answer is somewhere else. If you can recognize it in the moment, a short apology and an explanation can repair the damage, and you can find a better way to deal with the real source.

Sigmund Freud shaped the vocabulary of psychology, and we still talk about the unconscious, repression and the importance of early childhood. Many of his ideas entered everyday speech so thoroughly that we forget where they came from.
Some of those ideas hold up in modified forms. Others, such as the Oedipus complex or the idea that dreams are disguised wishes, have not been supported by evidence. A big problem is that many of his claims can't be tested, since any result can be explained within the theory. He's more important as a historical figure than as a scientific authority. It's fair to say that he asked some good questions, and that most of his answers have been replaced.

The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator sorts people into 16 types, such as INFJ or ESTP, from four either-or choices. It's very popular in workplaces, and many people enjoy finding out their type. It gives you a vocabulary for talking about differences.
But scientists generally don't regard it as reliable. In some studies, about half of people got a different type when they retook the test five weeks later. The reason is that traits like introversion fall along a continuum, with most people in the middle, and the test cuts the line in half. A person just under the line and a person just over it are labeled as opposites. The Big Five model has a much better record, and it describes people with scores and not boxes.

After decades of research, many personality psychologists settled on five broad dimensions: openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. Researchers have found the same five in many countries and languages, which suggests that they capture something real.
They stay fairly stable through adult life, and they predict real outcomes, such as job performance, relationship satisfaction and health. Unlike the Myers-Briggs types, each is measured on a scale, so most people are somewhere in the middle. Nobody is simply an extravert or an introvert. They're somewhere along the line, and that can vary a little with the situation. None of the five is good or bad in itself, though each has its own strengths and costs.

In 2015 Tinca Polderman and her colleagues combined nearly fifty years of twin studies, covering over 14 million pairs of twins. Across all the traits measured, about 49 percent of the differences between people could be traced to genes.
The other half came from the environment, mostly the kind that siblings in the same family don't share. That is a surprise to many, since we expect that growing up in the same house should make children alike. It means that neither genes nor upbringing alone decide who we become. It also reminds us that "heritable" doesn't mean "fixed." A trait can be partly genetic and still respond to what we do and what happens around us.

James Flynn discovered that the average score on IQ tests rose about three points every decade through most of the twentieth century, in many countries. That's a big change in a few generations, and it's too fast to be genetic.
Possible causes include more schooling, better nutrition and growing familiarity with abstract thinking and with tests. In some countries, scores have stopped rising or have even gone down in recent years, and experts aren't sure why. The Flynn effect is a good reminder that test scores are not a fixed measure of something inborn. They respond to the world a person grows up in, and a score from one generation can't be directly compared with one from another.

In 1983 the psychologist Howard Gardner proposed that people have several separate kinds of intelligence, such as musical, bodily, interpersonal and logical. The idea is very popular among teachers, and it feels generous, since it says that everyone is smart in some way.
But researchers haven't found good evidence that the types are independent. People who score high on one kind of mental test tend to score higher on others, which supports the idea of a general factor. The ideas are better seen as a way of appreciating different strengths than as a scientific theory of the mind. It's true that people have different talents. It's less clear that sorting students by "learning style" helps them learn.

In the 1960s and 70s Walter Mischel offered young children a choice: one marshmallow now, or two if they could wait. Follow-up studies suggested that the children who waited did better in life, with better test scores and fewer troubles. It became a famous story about willpower.
In 2018 Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan repeated the study with a larger and more varied group. After they took family background into account, the link was about half as strong, and mostly disappeared. Waiting seems to reflect circumstances as much as willpower. A child who has learned that adults keep their promises has good reason to wait, and one who has learned otherwise has good reason to eat the marshmallow.

In 2007 Angela Duckworth and her colleagues defined grit as passion and perseverance for long-term goals. They found that it predicted who stayed at West Point and who won the national spelling bee, and the idea quickly became popular.
Later reviews found that grit overlaps a lot with conscientiousness, a long-known trait, and predicts success only modestly. Perseverance does matter, but the idea that grit is a separate and powerful predictor has been oversold. It's still a useful thing to value in yourself. Just don't expect it to explain everything, and remember that sticking with something isn't always wise. Sometimes the grittiest thing to do is to stop and try something else.

In 1943 Abraham Maslow proposed that human needs form a pyramid, from physical needs and safety at the bottom to belonging, esteem and self-fulfillment at the top. You were supposed to satisfy each level before moving up.
The idea that needs matter is useful. The strict order isn't supported. A survey across more than 120 countries found that people pursue love and purpose even when basic needs aren't fully met, and that the needs seem to matter in parallel. Think of the starving artist, or the family who share what little they have. The pyramid is better thought of as a rough guide to the kinds of things that people need than as a ladder.

In the 1980s and 90s it was widely believed that raising children's self-esteem would improve their grades and behavior. Schools introduced programs and praise on that basis. In 2003 Roy Baumeister and his colleagues reviewed the research and found little to support it.
They found that self-esteem tends to follow success more than cause it, and that boosting it directly did little for performance. Praise for effort and strategy works better than praise for being smart, because it teaches that the outcome depends on what you do. That doesn't mean being harsh. It means that real accomplishments and honest feedback are a better foundation than hollow compliments. Self-respect that's earned lasts longer than self-esteem that's handed out.

In 1961 Stanley Milgram, at Yale, had volunteers play the part of a teacher who gave electric shocks to a "learner" for wrong answers, with the shocks increasing to a dangerous 450 volts. The shocks were fake, and the learner was an actor. The volunteers did not know this.
In the baseline version, 65 percent of participants went all the way to the maximum. Later analyses question how realistic the setup was, and how many participants really believed it. Still, it showed how far ordinary people may go under instruction from an authority, and many of the participants were visibly distressed as they did it. It's a sober reminder that "I was told to" is a weaker defense than it feels like.

In the early 1950s Solomon Asch asked people to say which of three lines matched a standard line, an easy task. But everyone else in the room was an actor and had been told to give the wrong answer. The real participant was the last to answer.
About 75 percent of the participants went along with the group at least once, and about a third of all their answers conformed. If one other person gave the right answer, conformity dropped sharply. A single ally makes it easier to speak up. That's a useful thing to know in a meeting or a family. If you disagree and are afraid to say so, someone else probably does too, and your voice may give them theirs.

In 1971 Philip Zimbardo had college students play guards and prisoners in a mock prison in a basement at Stanford. It was said to show that a situation turns ordinary people cruel, and it appeared in textbooks for decades.
But later evidence showed that the guards were coached on how to behave, and some participants were acting. In 2019 the researcher Thibault Le Texier published an analysis of the archives that raised serious doubts. Most psychologists now regard it as a vivid demonstration and not as proof of what happens naturally. It shows how powerful a setup can be, but it's a shaky basis for conclusions about human nature.

In 1954 Muzafer Sherif ran a summer camp for twenty-two boys in Oklahoma. He split them into two groups, the Rattlers and the Eagles, and set up competitions with prizes. Hostility rose quickly, with name-calling, raids and fights.
Later he created problems that could only be solved by working together, such as fixing the water supply, and the animosity eased. The study suggests that rivalry creates conflict and shared goals reduce it. Some critics have noted that Sherif tried other approaches before he got the result he wanted, so the study is less clean than its reputation. Still, it fits what many people have seen, that a common task can bring opponents together.

In 1966 Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser asked homeowners to put a large, ugly "Drive Carefully" sign on their lawns. Only about 17 percent agreed. That isn't surprising, since the sign was big and unattractive.
But when another group had earlier been asked to display a small sign, and had agreed, 76 percent said yes to the large one. A small yes changes how you see yourself, as someone who helps with this kind of thing, and it makes the next request easier. It's a technique that salespeople and fundraisers know well. If you notice that you're being led through a series of small agreements, it's fair to ask where the series is heading.

In 1975 Robert Cialdini and his colleagues asked college students to spend two years as volunteer counselors for juvenile offenders. Almost everyone said no, as you'd expect. The request was enormous.
When the same students were then asked to spend two hours taking the kids to the zoo, about half agreed, compared with 17 percent of students who were asked only about the zoo trip. After turning down a big request, people feel a pull to meet you partway. It's the opposite of the foot-in-the-door effect, and it relies on a sense of reciprocity: you gave a little, so I should give a little. It's worth knowing when you're negotiating.

In his 1984 book Influence, Robert Cialdini described six levers that make people say yes. Reciprocity means that we repay favors. Commitment means that we stay consistent with what we've said. Social proof means that we follow what others do. The others are authority, liking and scarcity.
He worked out the list by training with salespeople, fundraisers and advertisers, and observing what they did. Knowing the levers doesn't make you immune. But it helps you notice when someone is pulling one, and ask yourself whether you would agree without it. A "limited time only" sign is scarcity. A free sample is reciprocity. Once you can name the lever, it's easier to decide for yourself.

The name comes from experiments in the 1920s and 30s at the Hawthorne Works, a Western Electric factory near Chicago. Workers' output seemed to rise when the lighting was changed, whichever way, which was taken to mean that people work harder when they know they're being watched.
In 2011 Steven Levitt and John List went back to the original data and found little evidence of such an effect in those studies. Being observed may well change behavior, and it probably does in some situations. But this famous example isn't solid, and the story has grown in the retelling. It's a case where a catchy name outlived the evidence, and it's worth remembering whenever a neat story is repeated without a check.

In 1973 David Rosenhan published "On Being Sane in Insane Places." He said that eight healthy people faked one symptom, hearing voices, to be admitted to psychiatric hospitals, and that once inside they acted normally but weren't discovered for weeks.
A 2019 investigation by the journalist Susannah Cahalan found evidence that he misreported some of the data and details, and that some of the accounts did not match his own notes. Doubts about how reliably psychiatric diagnosis was made then were reasonable, and the field did change. But the study itself isn't trustworthy. It's a useful case of a dramatic result that people wanted to believe, and that few ever checked.

In the 1950s Harry Harlow raised baby rhesus monkeys with two artificial mothers. One was made of wire and held a bottle, and the other was covered in soft cloth but gave no milk. You might expect the babies to prefer the one that fed them.
The babies clung to the cloth mother and went to the wire one only to feed. It showed that attachment grows from comfort and contact, not just from food. It changed how child-care experts thought about babies, and it helped end the advice to avoid cuddling children. The experiments were cruel and would not be done today, but their lesson, that closeness is a need and not a luxury, has lasted.

In the 1970s Mary Ainsworth devised a short laboratory test. A one-year-old is in a playroom with a parent. A stranger comes in, the parent leaves, and then the parent comes back. What the baby does at the reunion shows a pattern.
About 65 percent were securely attached, upset when the parent left and quickly comforted on return. The rest showed avoidant or anxious patterns, either ignoring the parent or clinging and not settling. The test has been used for decades to study attachment, and its patterns have been linked to later development. It doesn't label children for life, since the relationship can change. But it shows that a baby's trust in a caregiver is something real and measurable.

In 1987 Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver proposed that adult romantic relationships follow the same patterns as the bond between a baby and a caregiver. People are described as secure, anxious or avoidant in how they handle closeness.
An anxious person worries about being left, and an avoidant person feels uneasy when things get close. Attachment styles are partly stable but not fixed, and they can change with new relationships or therapy. Researchers now measure them on spectrums and not as fixed types. The idea is useful as a way of understanding your own patterns. But it's best used gently, since it's a tendency and not a destiny, and it says more about how you respond than about who you are.

After the fall of the Ceaușescu regime in 1989, thousands of Romanian children were found in overcrowded orphanages with very little care. The English and Romanian Adoptees study followed those who were adopted into British families.
Children adopted before six months of age mostly caught up. Those adopted later had more lasting difficulties with attention, relationships and thinking. It showed that severe early neglect has real effects, and that earlier rescue helps. It also showed that many children recovered a great deal in loving homes, even after a terrible start. Both parts matter. The first years are important, and children can heal, which is a message of real hope for anyone who works with children who have had a hard beginning.

Ivan Pavlov, a Russian physiologist studying digestion, noticed that his dogs started to salivate when they heard the footsteps of the assistant who fed them. The dogs were responding to something that merely came before the food.
He then paired a bell with food and found that the bell alone would produce salivation. A neutral signal that's linked with something meaningful comes to trigger the same response. The same thing happens in people. A song linked to a memory can bring back the feeling, and the smell of a hospital can make your stomach tighten. We rarely choose these links. They form on their own, and it's helpful to know that they have an ordinary explanation.

In 1898 Edward Thorndike put cats in puzzle boxes and found that actions that led to escape were repeated. He called it the law of effect. B. F. Skinner developed the idea in the 1930s with his "Skinner box," a cage in which animals could press a lever for food.
Behavior that's followed by something rewarding becomes more likely, and behavior followed by something unpleasant becomes less likely. Rewards usually change behavior faster and more lastingly than punishment does, since punishment tells you what not to do and not what to do instead. It's the idea behind training a dog and also behind a lot of advice for parents. Catching someone doing something right works better than only noticing mistakes.

B. F. Skinner found that how often you reward matters. When rewards come on an unpredictable schedule, like a slot machine, animals keep pressing the lever the longest, even after the rewards stop altogether.
We can see the same thing in many places: checking your phone to see whether anything new has arrived, or pulling to refresh a feed. The unpredictability makes the habit stick, which is why it's so hard to break. Many apps are designed with this in mind. A useful trick is to remove the trigger, by turning off notifications or putting the phone in another room, because it's easier to avoid the urge than to resist it once it has started.

When a learned response stops being rewarded, it fades. A dog stops salivating to a bell that no longer predicts food. But it's not erased. After a rest, the response often returns, which is called spontaneous recovery.
In people, a fear or habit that has faded can come back with stress, or in a new place. That can feel like starting over, but it isn't. The new learning is still there, and it usually returns more quickly. Researchers like Mark Bouton find that practicing the new learning in many different settings makes it last longer. If an old fear or craving comes back, it doesn't mean the progress was fake. It means the old pattern is not gone, only quiet.

In 1920 John Watson and Rosalie Rayner at Johns Hopkins showed a nine-month-old baby a white rat while making a loud noise behind him. After several pairings, the baby cried at the sight of the rat, and at other furry things.
It's a famous example of conditioned fear, and it appears in nearly every textbook. It's also an ethically troubling study with weak methods, and later accounts of what it proved are often exaggerated. The details have been disputed, and even who the child really was has been argued over since. It wouldn't be allowed now. It's worth knowing as a piece of history, and as a reminder that a very famous finding isn't always a strong one.

In 1961 Albert Bandura and his colleagues showed nursery-school children an adult either hitting a large inflatable doll or ignoring it. Later, the children were left alone in a room with the doll.
Those who had seen the adult attack it copied the same actions and even the same words. The study showed that children can learn by watching, without being rewarded themselves. It started a long debate on media violence, which hasn't been settled. What it clearly showed is how much young children learn from what the adults around them do, and how little of that has to be taught on purpose. Children are always watching, and what we do in front of them often speaks louder than what we say.

In 1948 Edward Tolman showed that rats don't simply learn a chain of left and right turns. After they had learned a maze, he blocked the usual route. Instead of getting confused, they chose a new route in the direction of the goal, as if they had a map in their heads.
The finding was important because it showed that animals, and so people, build mental representations of space and not only habits. It came at a time when many psychologists thought that behavior was only a chain of responses. Decades later, researchers found cells in the brain that fire at particular places, which gave Tolman's idea a physical basis. You carry a map of your neighborhood, and it isn't a list of turns.

In 1930 Edward Tolman and Charles Honzik put hungry rats in a maze. One group was fed at the end every time and got better quickly. A second group was never fed. A third wasn't fed until the eleventh day.
On the day food appeared, the third group suddenly performed as well as the rewarded rats. They had been learning the layout all along but showed it only when it became worth showing. We learn a lot without reward, and we may not know how much until something calls on it. It suggests that curiosity alone teaches. A child exploring a new house or an adult wandering a new city is learning, even though nothing seems to come of it.

In 2006 James Coan and his colleagues put married women in a brain scanner and told them they might get a mild electric shock. Those who held their husband's hand showed less activity in brain areas linked with threat than those who held a stranger's hand or no one's.
Physical contact with someone you trust seems to calm the body's alarm system, and the effect was bigger in happier marriages. It's a small, striking piece of evidence that comfort isn't only a feeling. It has measurable effects on the body. That's worth remembering when someone near you is frightened or grieving. A hand on a shoulder or a long hug can do something that words often can't.

For a long time, textbooks said that the human brain has 100 billion neurons. It was a round number that nobody had really counted. In 2009 the Brazilian scientist Suzana Herculano-Houzel and her colleagues found a different way to do it. They dissolved brain tissue into a uniform soup of cell nuclei and counted samples of it under the microscope.
They arrived at about 86 billion neurons, and roughly the same number of other cells. It's a smaller number than the legend, and it's still more than enough to be astonishing. If each neuron were a grain of sand, you'd have enough to fill several bathtubs. What matters more than the count is the wiring. Each neuron can connect to thousands of others, and it's the connections that make a mind.

Neurons don't touch. At the junction between two of them, called a synapse, there's a tiny gap. When a signal arrives, the first cell releases chemical messengers that cross the gap and tell the next cell whether to fire.
A single neuron can receive thousands of these connections. Learning works partly by strengthening some synapses and letting others fade, so what you do with your brain changes its physical wiring. That's how a skill you practice turns into something your body just knows. It also means that the brain is never finished. Each time you repeat something, you are making a few connections a little stronger, and each time you leave something alone, you are letting some of them go quiet.

A neuron's signal is a spike of electricity that either happens fully or doesn't happen at all. In 1952 Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley worked out how the spike travels along a nerve fiber. They used the huge nerve fiber of a squid, which was big enough to put electrodes inside.
A stronger stimulus doesn't make a bigger spike. It makes more spikes per second. So the brain's code for "louder" or "brighter" is "faster," like a Geiger counter clicking more rapidly when it gets closer to something radioactive. The two men later shared a Nobel Prize for the work. It's a nice example of how a basic question, answered with the right animal, can explain something about every nervous system, including your own.

Many of your nerve fibers are wrapped in a fatty coating called myelin, in the way that electrical wire has insulation. It makes signals travel dramatically faster, over 100 meters per second in the fastest fibers, compared with about a meter per second in bare ones.
The coating is added in gaps, with small bare spots between, and the signal jumps from one spot to the next. In multiple sclerosis, the immune system attacks the myelin, and messages slow down or stop getting through. It's why the disease can cause weakness, numbness and vision trouble. Myelination continues for years in childhood and adolescence, which is part of why young children's reactions are slower than adults'.

Neurons get the attention, but the brain has about as many other cells, called glia, and they do vital work. Astrocytes feed neurons and tidy up their chemical surroundings. Oligodendrocytes make myelin. Microglia act as the brain's cleaners and defenders.
"Glia" comes from the Greek word for glue, since early anatomists thought that was all they were, a kind of packing material. It's now known that they help shape how circuits work, and they're a very active area of research. Einstein's brain, famously, was found to have more glia per neuron in one region than average, though whether that means anything is unclear. The lesson is that the brain is a team of different cells, and the neurons are only some of the players.

Your brain is only about 2 percent of your body's weight, but it uses roughly 20 percent of its energy, whether you're thinking hard or lying on the couch. Much of that goes to keeping neurons ready to fire, like an engine idling.
Hard concentration adds only a small amount to the constant bill. So "thinking burns lots of calories" is mostly a myth, since your brain is expensive just for being on. A chess match won't do much for your waistline, though the long sitting and the snacks might not help. It also means that a tired brain isn't necessarily one that has run out of fuel. Fatigue has more to do with how the brain's chemistry and state shift than with an empty tank.

Most of the brain's signaling comes down to a push and a pull. Glutamate is the main excitatory messenger, telling neurons to fire. GABA is the main inhibitory one, telling them to calm down.
The balance between them matters a great deal. Too much push, and the brain can tip into seizures. Too little, and thinking and movement slow. A lot of medicines work by shifting that balance. Alcohol and many anti-anxiety drugs, for instance, partly work by boosting the effect of GABA, which is why they feel calming. It also explains why mixing such drugs can be dangerous, since two things that turn down the brain can turn it down too far.

Serotonin is often called the mood chemical, but most of it, about 90 percent, is actually in your gut, where it helps regulate digestion. It doesn't cross from the gut into the brain, which makes its own supply.
For decades people said that depression comes from low serotonin. A big review in 2022 found no consistent evidence for that simple idea. That doesn't mean serotonin is irrelevant, and many people are helped by medicines that act on it. It means that the story is much more complicated than a single chemical running low, and no one is sure exactly how those medicines work. Mood is the product of many systems, and neat one-chemical explanations are usually too good to be true.

Dopamine has a reputation as the pleasure chemical, but one of its most important jobs is helping you move. In Parkinson's disease, the cells that make dopamine in a deep part of the brain gradually die. People develop tremors and slowness, and find it hard to start movements.
A drug called L-dopa, which the brain turns into dopamine, can restore movement for a time, and it was one of the first great successes of brain chemistry. The story shows that dopamine isn't simply about feeling good. It helps you get going, whether that's reaching for a cup or reaching for a goal. When it's low, even simple actions can feel like pushing through mud.

Acetylcholine is the messenger a nerve uses to tell a muscle to contract, so every step you take depends on it. It also plays a role in attention and memory in the brain, where it helps you focus on what matters.
Some medicines for Alzheimer's disease try to keep its levels up. And botulinum toxin, the active ingredient in Botox, works by blocking its release, which is why it relaxes muscles and smooths wrinkles. In larger doses, the same toxin causes a dangerous paralysis, because the muscles that breathe stop getting the message. The chemical is both ordinary and powerful, a reminder that the same messenger is used across the body for very different jobs.

In the early 1970s scientists found that the brain has receptors that fit opium, which seemed odd. Why would we have receptors for a plant drug? The answer came in 1975, when John Hughes and Hans Kosterlitz isolated the body's own opioid-like molecules, which they named enkephalins.
Endorphins are the broader family. They're released during hard exercise, laughter and pain, and they may be part of why a good run can feel wonderful. The poppy drug works because it happens to resemble something we make ourselves. It's a good example of how a puzzle can lead to a discovery. The question was not "what does the poppy do?" but "what is this receptor for?"

The "love hormone" or "cuddle hormone" has had a lot of press. Oxytocin does help with childbirth and breastfeeding, and it plays a role in bonding. Those parts are well established.
But the claims about nasal sprays making people more trusting have been hard to repeat, and some studies found that it can also increase favoritism toward your own group. Its effects depend heavily on the situation and the person, so the nickname oversimplifies. It's best seen as one of many signals that tune how we react to others, and not a switch for love. A hug may feel good, but the chemistry behind the good feeling is more tangled than the headlines suggest.

Cortisol is the body's main stress hormone, but it's not just for emergencies. It follows a daily rhythm, peaking about 30 minutes after you wake up, which helps you get going, and dropping to its lowest at night.
Short bursts of it are helpful, since they mobilize energy and sharpen attention. When levels stay high for a long time, it can harm memory, immune function and sleep. Both the spike and the recovery matter. A healthy stress system rises to meet a challenge and then settles, like a wave. If you find yourself constantly keyed up, it's worth thinking about what would give your body a chance to come back down, such as a regular bedtime or a break in the afternoon.

When you sense danger, your adrenal glands, which sit on top of your kidneys, release adrenaline within seconds. It makes your heart pound, widens your airways, sends blood to your muscles and sharpens your senses, preparing you to fight or flee.
In the United States, it's often called epinephrine, which is the same chemical, and it's the active ingredient in an auto-injector for severe allergic reactions. That's no accident. Adrenaline opens the airways and raises blood pressure, which is exactly what someone in anaphylactic shock needs. The pounding heart you feel before a speech is the same chemistry. It isn't a sign that something is wrong. It's your body getting ready to do something hard.

The front part of your brain, behind your forehead, is where planning, impulse control and weighing of consequences largely happen. It's among the last areas to mature, continuing to develop into your mid-twenties, which helps explain teenage risk-taking.
Damage to it can leave a person's knowledge and intelligence intact, but make it very hard to plan, to hold back impulses and to carry things through. It's also very sensitive to fatigue and stress. When you're exhausted or upset, the prefrontal cortex is the first to falter, which is why you make poorer decisions late at night or in the middle of an argument. Good judgment depends partly on a rested, calm brain.

The amygdala is a pair of almond-shaped clusters deep in the brain that tag things as important, especially possible threats. A woman with damage to hers, known in the research as S.M., felt almost no fear and had trouble recognizing fear on faces.
But the amygdala isn't only about fear. It also responds to what's new, surprising or emotionally charged, whether it's good or bad. It helps decide what's worth remembering, which is part of why emotional events are recalled so well. The common picture of it as the "fear center" is a simplification. A better description is that it's a detector of what matters, and it tells the rest of the brain to pay attention.

The hippocampus, named for its seahorse shape, is crucial for forming new memories and for finding your way around. In 2000 Eleanor Maguire scanned London taxi drivers, who have to memorize thousands of streets, and found that the rear part of their hippocampus was larger than in other people.
The more years they had driven, the bigger it was. It suggests that the adult brain can change with demanding use. It's also one of the first regions affected in Alzheimer's disease, which is why trouble forming new memories and getting lost are among the early signs. It's a part of the brain that rewards exercise, and learning your way around a new city is good for it.

The cerebellum sits at the back of the brain and its name means "little brain." It's small, about 10 percent of the brain's volume, but it contains about 80 percent of its neurons. It smooths and times your movements, keeps your balance and helps you learn skills like riding a bike.
Researchers have also found that it takes part in language and thinking, so it does more than coordinate muscles. It seems to help the brain refine any process by comparing what was expected with what happened. People with cerebellar damage may not be paralyzed, but their movements become clumsy and shaky, like a person who has had too much to drink. It's a good example of a part that looks modest and turns out to do a great deal.

Think of the thalamus as a switchboard in the middle of your brain. Almost all of the signals from your senses, except smell, stop there on their way to the outer cortex. It helps decide what gets through.
It also plays a part in regulating attention and sleep. When you fall asleep, the thalamus reduces the flow of information to the cortex, which is partly why you stop noticing the sounds around you. When it's damaged, people can have trouble staying alert or may lose awareness altogether. It's a small structure with a huge job, and it explains why a sense can seem to "turn off" when you are concentrating or drowsy.

The hypothalamus is only about the size of an almond, but it keeps your body in balance. It monitors and adjusts body temperature, thirst, hunger, sleep cycles and the release of many hormones.
It's also the link between the brain and the hormone system, directing the pituitary gland. When you shiver, feel hungry or get sleepy in the evening, the hypothalamus is involved. A tiny cluster of cells in it acts as the master body clock, and it takes its cues from light. For something so small, it holds a great deal of influence over how you feel, and why you feel hungry or tired at certain times.

Deep in the brain, the basal ganglia help you choose which action to take and when. They're involved in starting and stopping movements, and in turning repeated behavior into habit.
Ann Graybiel's work showed that as a routine becomes automatic, these structures change their activity. They begin to treat the whole sequence as a single chunk that starts and ends with a signal. They're affected in Parkinson's disease, where movement is hard to start, and in Huntington's disease, which causes unwanted movements. When you drive home without remembering the trip, you're mostly relying on these structures, which handle the routine so the rest of the brain is free.

The corpus callosum is a thick bundle of about 200 million nerve fibers that connects the left and right halves of the brain and lets them share information. Without it, the two sides would have to work separately.
In the mid-twentieth century, doctors began cutting it in some people with severe epilepsy, to stop seizures from spreading across the brain. The operation often worked. These patients became the subjects of the famous split-brain studies, which taught us a lot about how the two sides work. Outside the lab, most of them led quite normal lives, because the two halves find ways to share what they know through other routes, such as hearing what the other side says.

The insula is a fold of cortex tucked deep inside the brain, and it listens to your body. It's active when you notice your heartbeat, feel nauseated, sense pain or experience disgust.
Many scientists think it helps turn raw signals from your body into emotions. A gut feeling, in a literal sense, may involve your insula. People who are better at sensing their own heartbeat tend to have stronger emotional reactions, and the insula is part of the explanation. It's a reminder that feelings have a physical side, and that paying attention to what your body says can be a way of understanding what you feel.

This region sits in the middle of the brain, curving around the front of the corpus callosum. It's a kind of conflict monitor. It becomes active when two responses compete, as when you have to name the ink color of the word "red" printed in blue.
It also lights up when you realize you've made a mistake, and when you feel social pain, such as being excluded. It seems to signal that something needs attention. That would explain why being left out can feel so much like physical hurt, since some of the same alarm is involved. The little jolt you feel when you catch an error before anyone else does is probably this region at work.

The brainstem connects the brain to the spinal cord, and it runs the basics: breathing, heartbeat, blood pressure, and the cycle of sleeping and waking. You don't have to think about any of it, and you couldn't stop it if you tried.
That's also why damage to the brainstem is so often fatal. A small injury here can be more serious than a much larger injury in the outer parts of the brain. It's the oldest part of the brain in evolutionary terms, and it's shared by all vertebrates. The thoughtful parts of the brain get most of the credit, but they depend completely on this small stalk below them.

In the 1930s the neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield, operating on patients who were awake, stimulated the surface of the brain with a small electrode and noted which part of the body moved. He mapped a strip of cortex where each body part has its own patch.
When drawn as a figure, it looks like a distorted little person with huge hands, lips and tongue, because those parts need the most precise control. The legs and trunk, by contrast, take up very little room. The map shows that the brain doesn't give space according to size, but according to need. A fingertip that can feel and move with great delicacy gets far more cortex than the whole of your back.

In 1861 the French doctor Paul Broca treated a man nicknamed "Tan," because that was nearly the only word he could say, although he could understand speech. After the man died, Broca examined his brain and found damage in a spot in the left frontal lobe.
People with damage there still understand language but speak slowly and with effort. It was one of the first clear links between a brain region and a mental function, and it began the modern effort to map the mind onto the brain. We now know that language involves wider networks than a single spot. But Broca's case remains a landmark, because it showed that something as human as speech has a physical home.

In 1874 the German doctor Carl Wernicke described patients who had a different problem from Broca's. They could speak fluently, but what they said made little sense, and they had trouble understanding others. Their damage was in a part of the left temporal lobe.
The two language areas are linked by a bundle of fibers, and the pair showed that language depends on a network, not on one spot. One area helps you make speech, and the other helps you understand it. When you hear a sentence and say a reply, both are working together. The contrast between the two kinds of damage helped scientists see that speaking and understanding are separate abilities, even though they feel like one.

When the connection between the two hemispheres is cut, strange things happen. Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga tested these patients in the 1960s. If a word was flashed to the right hemisphere, which can't speak, the patient said they'd seen nothing, yet their left hand could pick out the matching object.
Each half seemed to have its own knowledge, and the talking half had no idea what the other half knew. Gazzaniga found that the speaking half would readily invent an explanation for something the other half had done, without noticing that it was guessing. Sperry won a Nobel Prize in 1981 for the work. It raises a thought-provoking idea. Part of what we call our reasons may be stories that our mind tells afterward.

In 1848 a railroad worker named Phineas Gage was packing explosive powder when it went off and drove an iron rod through the front of his skull. He survived, and a doctor reported that he changed from a responsible man into an impulsive, profane one.
Later historians found that the story had been exaggerated over time. Gage recovered much of his ability, and spent years working as a stagecoach driver in Chile, which takes planning and self-control, so the full tale is more complicated than the textbooks suggested. His case still showed that damage to the front of the brain can change personality. But it's a good example of how a dramatic story can grow, and it's worth checking before repeating.

In some animals, the hippocampus keeps making new neurons through adulthood. Whether people do is hotly debated. It would be a hopeful finding, since it would mean that the adult brain can replace some of what it loses.
In 2018 one team reported that new neurons in the human hippocampus stop forming in childhood, and another team, in the same year, found evidence that they continue into old age. The different results may come from how brain samples were handled and how the cells were identified. So the answer, for now, is that nobody is sure. Be wary of claims that a food or a habit "grows new brain cells," since the basic fact is not settled.

A baby's brain has a burst of connection-building, and the number of synapses peaks in early childhood. Then, through adolescence and into early adulthood, the brain trims many of them, keeping the ones that are used.
It may sound like a loss, but it makes the circuits more efficient. Pruning is a bit like trimming a hedge. What you're left with is shaped by experience, which is a good reason to give children varied and rich surroundings. It also helps explain why a child picks up a language so easily and an adult finds it harder. The young brain is open to everything, and as it matures, it commits to what it has found useful.

A night of sleep isn't one steady state. Over about 90 minutes you go from light sleep into deep sleep and then into REM sleep, and then the cycle repeats four or five times in the night.
Deep sleep is concentrated in the first half of the night, and REM sleep gets longer toward morning. That's why cutting your sleep short on the end loses most of your REM, and it may be one reason you feel foggy. It also explains why going to bed very late and sleeping in is not the same as going to bed earlier. The stages come in a particular order, and each has its own work to do for your body and mind.

In 1953 Eugene Aserinsky, a graduate student, and his professor Nathaniel Kleitman noticed that sleepers' eyes darted back and forth under their lids at certain times in the night. When they woke people during that phase, they often reported vivid dreams.
It's called rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep. In REM, your body's muscles are mostly paralyzed, which keeps you from acting out your dreams. Sometimes the paralysis lingers for a moment when you wake, which can be frightening but is harmless. In a rare disorder, the paralysis fails, and people do act out their dreams. The sleeping brain is far from idle. In REM it's nearly as active as it is awake.

In 2013 Maiken Nedergaard's lab at the University of Rochester reported that, in mice, the spaces between brain cells expanded by about 60 percent during sleep. That let cerebrospinal fluid wash through and carry away waste, including proteins linked to Alzheimer's disease.
It suggested that one function of sleep is cleaning house. The evidence in people is still developing, and scientists are debating the details, including how the system works and how much it's affected by sleep. It's an attractive idea, and it fits what we know about the harm of poor sleep. But it's best held as a promising explanation and not a finished fact. For now, it's one more reason to take sleep seriously.

In 2015 the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society issued a consensus statement, based on a panel of experts reviewing the research. It said that adults should regularly sleep at least seven hours a night for good health.
Needs vary a little from person to person, and a few people truly do well on less. But for most of us, the evidence is that short sleep over time is linked with problems such as high blood pressure, weight gain and low mood. If you rely on caffeine to get through the day, you're probably not getting enough. It's one of the simplest and most effective things you can do for your health, and it costs nothing.
Sleep loss feels like being drunk

In studies from the late 1990s, researchers compared the effects of staying awake with the effects of alcohol. After 17 to 19 hours without sleep, people's performance on tests of reaction time and coordination was as poor as at a blood alcohol level of 0.05 percent.
After 24 hours it was like 0.10 percent, which is over the legal driving limit in the United States. The troubling part is that tired people often don't feel as impaired as they are, just as drunk people often don't. Drowsy driving is a real danger, and it causes many crashes every year. If you're very tired, the safest choice is to rest before you drive, and a coffee doesn't fix it.

Till Roenneberg, a German chronobiologist, found that many people sleep much later on weekends than on workdays. He called the mismatch "social jetlag," because it's like flying a few time zones west on Friday night and back east on Monday morning, without ever leaving home.
People with a bigger gap between their workday and weekend sleep tend to be more tired and in a worse mood, and to have more health problems. The body clock doesn't adjust instantly, so Monday morning can feel like the middle of the night. Keeping a regular wake-up time, even on days off, helps. If you have to catch up on sleep, it's better to go to bed earlier than to sleep in much later.
The body clock is not exactly 24 hours

Your internal clock runs slightly longer than a day. In 1999 Charles Czeisler and his colleagues kept volunteers in dim light for weeks, with no clocks and no daylight cues, and measured an average internal day of 24 hours and 11 minutes.
Each morning, light resets the clock to the 24-hour day. That's why a bright morning can make you feel better, and why jet lag takes days to clear. It also explains why many people drift later when they don't have a reason to get up. Without the daily nudge from light, the clock slips a few minutes every day. A walk outside in the morning, even on a cloudy day, is one of the best ways to keep your clock on schedule.

During puberty, the body clock moves later. Mary Carskadon at Brown University found that teenagers don't get sleepy until later in the evening, and naturally want to wake later in the morning, and it isn't just laziness. It's biology.
When schools have started later, studies have found that students got more sleep and had better attendance. A 7:30 start asks a teenager to wake at what feels like the middle of their night. If you live with a teenager, it may help to remember that the grumpy morning isn't defiance. Their clock is running behind the school's, and you can help by keeping the evening screens down and the bedroom dark, but you can't fully fight their biology.

The retina of each eye has two kinds of light sensors. Rods, about 120 million of them, work in dim light but can't see color, which is why the world looks gray at night. Cones, about 6 million, work in bright light and give you color and fine detail.
The cones are concentrated in the center of your vision, where you focus. That's why you can't read out of the corner of your eye, and why a faint star seems to vanish when you look straight at it, but reappears when you look slightly to one side. The two systems together let us see in both starlight and sunshine, a range of brightness that spans many millions to one.

Each eye has a place where the optic nerve leaves the back of the eye, and there are no light sensors there. So each of us has a small hole in our vision. We don't notice it, because the brain fills it in using the surroundings and the other eye.
You can find yours. Close your left eye, look at a mark on the left side of a page with your right eye, and move the page slowly toward you until a second mark to its right disappears. The brain doesn't just ignore the gap. It paints over it with whatever pattern is nearby, so what you see there is a guess. It's a small, neat reminder that vision is something the brain builds and not a window.

Your eyes don't glide smoothly across a scene. They hop about three times a second, in quick jumps called saccades, and stop to take in information between the jumps. If you watch someone's eyes as they read, you can see the hops.
During each jump, your vision is briefly suppressed, so you don't see the blur. What feels like a smooth, continuous view is in fact built from many snapshots stitched together by your brain. You can test it by looking in a mirror and trying to watch your own eyes move from one to the other. You'll never see them move, because you're blind during the jump. Someone else would.

Thomas Young proposed in 1802 that the eye has three kinds of color receptors, and later experiments confirmed it. Each type of cone responds best to a different range of light, roughly red, green and blue, and your brain compares their signals to give you the full range of colors.
Yellow, for instance, isn't detected by a yellow sensor. It's what the brain makes when the red and green cones are both stimulated. About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have a form of color blindness, because the genes involved are on the X chromosome, and men have only one copy of it. Most people with it can see colors, but they confuse certain pairs, such as red and green.

The cochlea, a coiled tube in the inner ear that looks like a snail shell, is where sound turns into nerve signals. It's lined with thousands of tiny hair cells, each tuned to a certain pitch, a little like the keys on a piano.
In humans, once those cells are destroyed, they don't grow back, which is why damage from loud noise is permanent. Young people can hear from about 20 to 20,000 hertz, and the upper range shrinks with age. By middle age, many people can no longer hear the highest tones, though everyday speech is mostly unaffected at first. The hair cells you have now are the ones you'll have for life, which is worth remembering the next time you are close to a loud speaker.

Sounds at 85 decibels, about as loud as heavy city traffic, can damage hearing if you hear them for hours. For every 3 decibels louder, the safe time is cut in half. So the louder the sound, the sooner it does harm.
A rock concert at 100 decibels is safe for only about 15 minutes without protection. Hearing loss from noise builds up silently and permanently, and the first sign is often a ringing in the ears after a loud event. A pair of cheap foam earplugs makes a real difference, and so does standing a little further from the speaker. The earlier you protect your hearing, the more of it you will have in old age.

Your tongue detects five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. The Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda identified umami in 1908, when he worked out what made seaweed broth so savory. It's the taste of glutamate, found in broth, cheese and ripe tomatoes.
You may have seen a "tongue map" with different zones for each taste. It's a myth, and every area of the tongue can detect all five. The idea came from a misreading of an old German paper. Most of what we call flavor is really smell, which is why food tastes bland when you have a cold. The tongue gives you a few simple signals, and the nose adds the thousands of subtle shades.

The sense of smell has a more direct route to the brain's emotional and memory areas than the other senses do. Scent signals reach the amygdala and the hippocampus after only a couple of connections.
That may be why a smell, like a perfume or a kitchen, can suddenly bring back a vivid scene from childhood. Studies find that odor-evoked memories tend to be more emotional, though they aren't necessarily more accurate. The evidence for the idea that smell is special is mixed, so it's best held as a likely but unproven link. Still, many people can name a scent that takes them straight back to a place, and it's a pleasant thing to notice.

In 2014 a study in Science claimed that humans can tell apart more than a trillion different odors. It was a striking number and it got a lot of press, since it seemed to overturn the old idea that people have a poor sense of smell.
Other scientists looked at the math and said that the conclusion didn't follow from the data, and that the true number could be far lower, perhaps only in the thousands. We still don't know how many smells people can really distinguish. It's a good lesson in reading headlines about big numbers. A surprising figure from a single study is an invitation to look further, not a fact to repeat.
The gate control theory of pain

In 1965 Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall proposed that the spinal cord has a kind of gate that can let pain signals through or block them. Signals from touch, for example, can close the gate, which is why rubbing a bumped elbow helps.
Signals from the brain can also open or close it, so your attention, mood and expectations change how much a given injury hurts. Soldiers wounded in battle sometimes report little pain, and a stubbed toe hurts more when you're already upset. The theory isn't exactly right in its details, but its main message holds. Pain isn't just a signal that goes straight to the brain. It's shaped on the way, and what's going on in your mind matters.

After an amputation, many people go on feeling the missing limb, sometimes with pain. It can feel as real as the limb did, and a person may reach out with it or feel it clench.
V. S. Ramachandran invented a mirror box in the 1990s. A patient puts the intact hand in one side so that its reflection looks like the missing one, then moves it, and some felt relief from the pain. Later trials have had mixed results, so it's an interesting idea that works for some people and not others. The phenomenon itself is well documented. It shows that the brain keeps a map of the body, and that the map doesn't go away when the part does.

Close your eyes and touch your nose. You can do it because of a sense you rarely notice, proprioception, which tells you where your limbs are. In 1906 the physiologist Charles Sherrington gave it its name.
Stretch sensors in your muscles, tendons and joints send constant information to the brain. People who lose it, from nerve disease, have to watch their limbs to move them at all. If they close their eyes, they collapse. It's the quiet sense behind walking in the dark, typing without looking and catching a ball. Practicing movements, as in yoga or dance, can sharpen it, and so can balance exercises, which become more important as you age.

Deep in each inner ear are three fluid-filled loops that sense rotation of the head, and two small organs that sense tilt and acceleration. Together they're the vestibular system, which keeps you balanced and your gaze steady as you move.
When you turn your head, the fluid sloshes, and the brain uses the signal to move your eyes the opposite way, so the world doesn't blur. Motion sickness happens when the signals from this system don't match what your eyes see, as when you read in a moving car, so your brain gets conflicting reports. That's why looking out the window at the horizon helps. It gives your eyes and your ears the same story.

Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day without a break. At rest it pumps about five liters of blood around the body each minute, which is roughly all the blood you have, so a drop of blood makes a complete trip in about a minute.
Over a long lifetime it will beat more than 2.5 billion times. It's a muscle, and regular exercise makes it stronger and more efficient. A trained athlete's resting heart rate can be as low as 40 beats per minute, because each beat moves more blood. It's the one muscle that never rests, and it's worth looking after. A brisk walk each day is one of the kindest things you can do for it.

Skin is the body's largest organ, covering about two square meters in an adult. It keeps water in and germs out, helps regulate your temperature, makes vitamin D when exposed to sunlight, and gives you the sense of touch.
The outer layer constantly sheds and replaces itself, about once a month, so some of the dust in a home is shed skin. When you're hot, the skin sweats, and when you're cold, its blood vessels narrow to save heat. It's easy to take for granted, since we only notice it when it goes wrong, but it's a remarkable coat. It heals itself, it repairs cuts, and it is waterproof and flexible at the same time.

The liver can do something no other internal organ does: regrow. If part of it is removed, as in surgery or in a living donation, the remainder can grow back to nearly the original size within weeks.
It's also a chemical workhorse that filters the blood, makes bile for digesting fat, stores sugar and breaks down drugs and toxins. It's why living-donor liver transplants are possible. A healthy person can give a portion to someone who is sick, and both livers grow to a useful size. The Greek myth of Prometheus, whose liver was eaten each day and grew back each night, may hint that the ancients knew something about it.

Your two kidneys filter about 180 liters of fluid from your blood each day, far more than the volume of fluid in the body. Almost all of it is reclaimed, leaving about 1.5 liters to leave as urine.
The kidneys keep the balance of salts and water just right, and help control blood pressure. Each one has about a million tiny filters.
